☆ Nonreciprocal Josephson Dynamics of a $\mathcal{PT}$-Symmetric Atomtronic SQUID
Nalinikanta Pradhan, Rina Kanamoto, M. Bhattacharya, Pankaj K. Mishra
We investigate non-Hermitian Josephson dynamics in an atomtronic quantum interference device (AQUID), formed by a ring Bose Einstein condensate with balanced atomic gain and loss regions and two moving optical barriers. The balanced gain and loss profile establishes a parity time symmetric potential while breaking spatial inversion symmetry, providing the essential ingredients for nonreciprocal Josephson transport. The dynamics are monitored nondestructively through the phase quadrature spectrum of an optomechanical cavity driven by Laguerre Gaussian beams coupled to the condensate. We demonstrate that increasing the local gain and loss strength softens the parity time symmetric collective mode towards an exceptional point, as verified by Bogoliubov de Gennes analysis. The associated coherent population exchange produces an additional characteristic splitting in the cavity output spectrum. For linearly translating barriers, non-Hermiticity provides an additional control parameter for tuning the critical current. When the barriers undergo simultaneous translation and rotation, the rotation induced phase modifies the interference between counter propagating currents, offering further control over the nonreciprocal response. Under periodic barrier modulation, we find more pronounced Shapiro steps in the current voltage characteristics due to the intrinsic parity time symmetric collective mode. Finally, we propose an alternative Hermitian realization using a tilted optical lattice, providing an experimentally accessible route to engineering biased transport and population transfer. Our results establish parity time symmetric atomtronic SQUIDs as a versatile platform for controlling nonreciprocal Josephson transport and collective excitations in driven quantum fluids.

☆ Intracycle Interference in Strong-Field Photoemission from a Tungsten Needle Tip
Timo Wirth, Jonas Heimerl, Stefan Meier, Peter Hommelhoff
Electrons photoemitted by strong laser fields can rescatter, generating attosecond high harmonics. Spectral peaks arise from inter- and intracycle interference of coherent electron wave packets. While intercycle interference is well known, intracycle interference of plateau electrons has not been observed. We present carrier-envelope phase-resolved photoemission spectra from a nanometric tungsten needle tip driven at 1570 nm revealing such interference, supported by quantum orbit and TDSE simulations that elucidate attosecond-scale electron dynamics.

☆ Two atoms with strong light-induced dipolar interactions
Hanzhen Lin, Yoo Kyung Lee, Nabeel Rasheed, Vitaly Fedoseev, Cicely Motamedi, Wolfgang Ketterle
We study how two atoms scatter light when they are closer than an optical wavelength and observe multiple new phenomena due to the strong interactions between laser-induced electric dipole moments. We identify a narrow range of densities where a fraction of the scattered light is coherent and shows a collective enhancement factor of two compared to independent atoms. The dynamics of the two-atom wavefunction can be observed through momentum distributions which reveal resonant ejection and depletion. Due to the tight confinement, the total fluorescence intensity strongly depends on the scattering length, since it originates from a narrow resonant (Franck-Condon) region. Furthermore, we measure how the probe laser intensity modifies the scattering length, which establishes a new way to shift Feshbach resonances. Our work provides microscopic insight into what occurs during photoassociation and parity projection in optical tweezers.

☆ Additively manufactured ceramic platforms for miniaturized optical frequency references and robust atomic sensor systems SP
Marc Christ, Sascha Neinert, Conrad Zimmermann, Klaus Döringshoff, Markus Krutzik
Transferring atomic quantum sensors from laboratory-scale physics packages to compact, alignment-free sensor heads suitable for field and space deployment requires a structural platform that combines mechanical, thermal, and optical functionality within a single, manufacturable component. We present such a platform based on additively manufactured technical ceramics: lithography-based ceramic manufacturing is used to fabricate monolithic micro-optical benches with application-specific mounting geometries, while high-precision active alignment and adhesive bonding realize long-term stable optical assemblies through micro-integration. As a first system-level demonstrator, we present a micro-integrated optical frequency reference based on Doppler-free spectroscopy of the rubidium D2 line, integrated within a 6 mL Al2O3 module. A laser stabilized to the reference reaches a fractional frequency instability of $3\times10^{-12}$ at 1 s. We extend the platform to a compact optically pumped magnetometer, exploiting the magnetic cleanliness and tailored thermal properties of high-purity ceramics for a 7 mL sensor head with picotesla sensitivity aimed at space-borne biomagnetometry, and to a micro-integrated optical dipole trap with active MEMS-mirror beam steering for cold-atom manipulation. Together, these demonstrators show that ceramic additive manufacturing and optical micro-integration form a versatile, robust platform for compact atomic sensor systems in field and space applications.

☆ Observation of strong electric dipole-dipole interactions between two atoms
Yu-Kun Lu, Jiahao Lyu, Wolfgang Ketterle
We have prepared pairs of atoms at densities exceeding $ 10^{16}/\rm{cm}^3$ corresponding to $n\lambdabar^3>10$ and studied how they interact with light. In this regime, the coherent part of the electric dipole-dipole interaction is larger than the dissipative part, and a single photon emission can transfer large momenta (larger than ten times the single photon recoil) to the atoms. For off-resonant laser light, the atoms are dressed with an electric dipole moment of $\approx$ 1 Debye and interact coherently. This light-induced dipole-dipole interaction has been previously observed only in the far-field mean-field regime. For two atoms, the resonance is shifted by the two-body Lamb shift which is dominated by the near-field part of the dipolar interaction. Dipolar resonance shifts have been observed before only for many atoms interacting with the far-field part of the dipolar interaction. Our work sheds new light on photoassociation processes and paves the way for studying driven quantum systems with strong electric dipole-dipole interactions.
♻ ☆ Efficient photo-ionizing elimination of detrimental electric fields for Rydberg atoms
Zhou-Chen Deng, Hao-Nan Lin, Yu-Cheng Duan, Qi Zhang, Xiang-Can Cheng, Yang Liu, Zhao-Yang Yuan, Jie Li, Peng Liu, Zhan Wu, Chao-Yang Lu, Jun Rui, Jian-Wei Pan
Rydberg atoms are highly sensitive to external electric fields due to their exaggerated electronic properties. This unique feature underpins many of their applications in quantum science. However, uncontrolled stray electric fields can be detrimental, severely degrading quantum control. In this work, we demonstrate a novel scheme that efficiently creates an in-vacuum charge source by photo-ionizing laser-cooled atoms and eliminates detrimental electric fields in a Rydberg-atom tweezer array platform, using only readily available resources. With this method, we began with Stark-ionized Rydberg continuum spectra caused by a large, unknown stray electric field of more than $10~\mathrm{V/cm}$ and ultimately recovered well-resolved coherent excitation of individual Rydberg states after eliminating the residual field to an upper limit of $20(1)~\mathrm{mV/cm}$. Our method applies directly to existing Rydberg-atom platforms and other experiments sensitive to stray electric fields.

☆ Nonperturbative string dynamics in a (2+1)D lattice gauge theory on a superconducting quantum processor
Sanziana Stelea, Anthony Gandon, Francesco Tacchino, Jad C. Halimeh, Ivano Tavernelli
Electric flux strings underpin confinement in gauge theories. In two spatial dimensions, their evolution involves competing processes of charge motion, pair creation, and transverse deformation. Accessing these dynamics beyond perturbative limits challenges classical approaches, as entanglement growth restricts the times accessible to tensor-network simulations. Here we use quantum simulation to investigate a (2+1)D Z2 lattice gauge theory with dynamical matter and an explicit magnetic plaquette interaction, spanning strongly confined and nonperturbative deconfined regimes. Using 63 superconducting qubits, including 12 ancillas, we evolve initially localized strings with static or dynamical endpoint charges. Spatially resolved measurements reveal rapid charge and flux spreading in the deconfined regime, enhanced matter occupation in the string interior near the pair-creation resonance, and suppressed spreading at strong electric fields. String-path occupations further probe transverse rearrangements between configurations connected by plaquette operations. Retaining separate matter and gauge degrees of freedom makes local Gauss-law constraints directly accessible for error detection. Combining these constraints with ancilla checks and noise rescaling, we measure dynamics in circuits containing up to 15 second-order Trotter steps. Our results establish quantum simulation as a practical approach to exploring nonperturbative string dynamics in two spatial dimensions, with gauge redundancy serving as an experimental resource.
☆ Finite-Key Readiness and Authentication-Key Replenishment in QKD-Assisted UAV Edge Computing
Dang H. Le, Ban Q. Tran, Susan Mengel
A service that needs fresh quantum keys must wait for key release, and may be denied it, before protected computation starts. We quantify this cost for a trusted stationary UAV serving two ground gateways, each obtaining its keys from one finite-key decoy-state BB84 attempt with parameters fixed in advance. A count-level Monte Carlo model, reproduced by a semi-analytic model, links key acceptance to protected upload, computation, and download, including failed attempts and hover energy. At 26~dB effective optical loss, with authentication hashing at its proxy-benchmarked, near-zero cost, fresh keys raise the 95th-percentile completion time of both tasks from 10.37 to 28.65~s; hover energy grows in proportion. The scalar rate models evaluated here miss the deadline limit on the block size. The pulse budget lies in a window bounded below by authentication-key replenishment and above by the deadline; for a fixed source, channel, and acceptance model, the authentication debit shifts the floor, whereas hashing cost does not. At a 35-s deadline the largest tested loss with a non-empty window is 27~dB at 1\% misalignment and 22~dB at 2\%; at 3\% no tested setting has one. Conditional on the assumed acquisition probability, the selected configurations meet this deadline with simultaneous lower confidence bounds of 96.9--97.3\% on held-out trials, at 26~dB and at 18--20~dB with 2\% misalignment. A high-cost stress reference that charges hashing in full narrows the window and lowers these loss limits to 26 and 20~dB at the reference processing capacity. A small rise in error rate or loss pushes the deadline probability well below its target and drains authentication keys, while the protocol's security parameter is unchanged.

☆ Structure of correlations for the single-$j$ model using quantum information theory
Javier Faba, Vicente Martín, Luis Robledo
We say that a system undergoes a quantum phase transition when the mean-field ground state of a given Hamiltonian spontaneously breaks its symmetries depending on the Hamiltonian parameters. It is a widely accepted view that this phenomenon enables the mean-field state to absorb the maximum amount of correlations without losing its mean-field structure. However, it is still uncertain how those correlations are incorporated within the mean-field state and how the correlation structure changes when we get closer to the exact ground state by restoring the symmetries. In this work, we answer these questions by studying the single-$j$ model, which is a realistic fermionic nuclear model with abelian and non-abelian broken symmetries. We find that both types of symmetries have very different effects for the correlations within the mean-field state. This makes unclear the concept of the symmetry breaking process as a mechanism to absorb the maximum amount of correlations. Moreover, the symmetry restoration redistributes existing `fake' correlations between paired orbitals to more complex subsystems.

☆ Quantum Thermal Transistor via Nonlinear Environmental Coupling
Laiba Hayat, M. Tahir Naseem
Thermal amplification enables sensitive control of heat currents, providing a basis for heat management and thermal signal processing in quantum devices. For a harmonic oscillator coupled to emitter, collector, and base thermal reservoirs, we recover the absence of thermal amplification when system-reservoir interactions permit only single-quantum exchange. A controlled weak-nonlinearity expansion, supported by numerical stationary solutions, shows that two-quantum exchange at the emitter enables amplification and predicts its onset. When two-quantum exchange dominates at the emitter and collector, varying the base temperature redistributes populations between even and odd oscillator sectors. This changes the emitter and collector heat currents far more than the base current, enabling large thermal amplification. We propose a realization using a longitudinally coupled auxiliary two-level system and bath spectral filtering, specifying conditions for its elimination to yield the required oscillator dynamics. These results establish nonlinear system-reservoir coupling as a resource for controlling heat flow and enabling thermal amplification.
☆ The energetic cost of loading classical data in quantum computers
Joao F. Doriguello, Alessandro Luongo, Harshit Verma
Quantum algorithms for machine learning, chemistry, and cryptanalysis often assume coherent access to classical data at negligible physical cost. We instead treat data loading as a hardware process and quantify the dynamic energetic cost of a quantum random access memory (QRAM) query on a superconducting processor. Using the metric-noise-resource framework, we relate query fidelity and power to gate duration, relative two-qubit drive strength, and the distribution of attenuation across a multi-stage refrigerator, while accounting for thermal photons and gate errors. We analyze the linear-depth multiplexer and the noise-resilient bucket-brigade architectures, adapting the latter to a native superconducting gate set and refining its fidelity analysis using the fully decomposed gate schedule. For a representative bucket-brigade QRAM query with a $12$-qubit address register we obtain a query fidelity of $0.969$. The query consumes $3.51\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{J}$ of dynamic energy, corresponding to an average dynamic power of $4.38\,\mathrm{W}$ and a peak of $64.4\,\mathrm{W}$. Our optimization shows that, at fixed target fidelity, the operating point and attenuation profile can change the average power by a factor of two or more.
☆ Multidimensional Quantum Block Turbo Codes
Khaled Jebari, Luiz Anet Neto, Ramesh Pyndiah, Jean-Louis de Bougrenet de la Tocnaye
The theory of turbo iterative decoding was brought into the quantum coding framework through the development of quantum serial turbo codes and quantum block turbo codes. In this paper, we present a theory for multidimensional quantum block turbo codes, a turbo decoding technique for multi layer product codes. We describe its algorithm and simulate the performance for the 3D case on a depolarizing channel.
☆ Simulating closed- and open-system dynamics of Tavis--Cummings lattices on fault-tolerant quantum computers
Soumya Sarkar, Rakshit Gharat, Nam Nguyen, Gavin Brennen
Tavis--Cummings lattices couple cavities containing several emitters and host polaritonic many-body dynamics whose real-time correlations are costly to compute classically in two dimensions, especially when unequal emitter relaxation or dephasing rates break permutation symmetry. We analyze logical resources for fault-tolerant closed- and open-system simulation of an atom-resolved lattice with $L$ cavities, $N$ emitters per cavity, and photon cutoff $n\_{\max}$, including target observable estimation. Building on ladder-operator block encoding, we construct circuits for photon hopping and local light--matter exchange and combine them to encode the lattice Hamiltonian. By updating source and destination photon occupations in place, the hopping circuit eliminates the auxiliary $L\lceil\log_2(n\_{\max}+1)\rceil$-qubit photon register used by two-register implementations. Across three uniform-coefficient examples with $16$ to $256$ cavities, the controlled walk uses $4.75$--$8.11%$ fewer Toffoli gates than the paired two-register implementation under matched shared preparation, precision, control, and workspace conventions. For closed systems, we implement real-time evolution with generalized quantum signal processing and bound the cost of estimating retarded cavity spectral functions. For open systems with photon loss, emitter relaxation, and dephasing, we use a sampled first-order dilation and bound the runs and timesteps needed to estimate transient photon statistics such as $g^{(2)}(0)$. With state-preparation and measurement costs explicit, these estimates provide a reference for assessing fault-tolerant light--matter lattice simulation costs.

☆ Implementing rapid reset of superconducting qubits with on-chip dissipation
Feiyu Li, Yang Liu, Zhen Yang, Zhenxing Liu, Jiayu Ding, Yang Gao, Xuehui Liang, Weijie Sun, Yanjun Ma, Chuhong Yang, Guangming Xue, He Wang, Fei Yan
Rapid and high-fidelity qubit reset is essential for quantum state initialization and quantum error correction. Conventional reset protocols for superconducting qubits often rely on dissipative elements connected to external circuitry, exposing qubits to thermal noise from higher-temperature environments. Here, we experimentally demonstrate a scalable approach to qubit reset and leakage removal over multiple transmon qubits using dedicated dissipation units comprising resonators coupled to on-chip resistive loads. This architecture provides Purcell protection while isolating the qubits from warmer external circuitry. We achieve a median reset time constant of approximately 48 ns for the $|g\rangle-|e\rangle$ transition, with an effective bath temperature of 30 mK. A 400-ns reset pulse yields residual excited-state populations of $0.29\%$ and $0.67\%$ for qubits initialized in $|g\rangle$ and $|e\rangle$, respectively. We further demonstrate efficient leakage removal from the $|f\rangle$ state, reducing its residual population to $0.51\%$. These results establish a simple, reproducible, and easy-to-integrate approach to dissipation engineering in superconducting quantum processors.
☆ Operational limits of reference renewal for retained quantum-service results
Roberto Fernández-Barrios, Iker Pastor-López, Amaia Pikatza-Huerga, Pablo García Bringas
We implement reference renewal to reconsider retained physical quantum-service results under a prespecified protocol. Twelve transitions retained six results each; ten completed renewal, eight met the prespecified endpoint, and five succeeded using retained results alone. The exact one-sided p=0.0546875 does not establish the recovery hypothesis. Incomplete references, binding failures and sequential waits expose operational limits. Offline reconstruction recovers decisions from preserved counts. Retrospective binding-plus-oracle checking accepts all 60 usable-transition results without renewal. With the exact oracle also supplying calibration scores, the study does not demonstrate incremental numerical-correctness utility of renewal.

☆ Invariance can prevent overfitting and shortcut learning in Quantum Neural Networks
Giuseppe D'Ambruoso, Giovanni Gramegna, Domenico Pomarico, Giuseppe Magnifico, Cosmo Lupo
Many image classification tasks have labels that are unchanged by rotations and reflections. Equivariant quantum neural networks incorporate such symmetries by design, but the specific benefit of symmetry is difficult to isolate. Equivariant quantum circuits are usually compared with architectures that also differ in gates, structure or size. Here, we investigate the role of invariance in a controlled setting, classifying images whose labels are invariant under the dihedral group $D_4$. We compare four eight-qubit models with identical encoding, circuit structure and number of trainable parameters, and equivalent dynamical Lie algebras, and benchmark invariant implementations against non-invariant ones in terms of generalization error, robustness to shortcut learning and resilience to a realistic noise model. On four binary tasks, including MNIST and two scientific data sets of galaxies and red blood cells, the invariant models trained on a few tens of images show better generalization than non-invariant ones. Invariance also makes the models immune to orientation shortcuts: when trained with a class-dependent corner watermark, the non-invariant models learn the watermark and often drop to chance level when it is moved. We show that the gain in accuracy of invariant models persists also under a realistic noise model.
☆ High-Speed Control of a Fluxonium Qubit via Picosecond Pulses from Josephson Digital Circuits
M. V. Bastrakova, D. S. Pashin, V. A. Vozhakov, N. V. Klenov, I. I. Soloviev
We develop a control strategy for fluxonium qubits based on picosecond single-flux-quantum (SFQ) pulses generated by Josephson digital circuits. A major challenge is that SFQ protocols originally designed for transmon control become inefficient for low-frequency fluxonium. In this regime, the asymmetry of flux and charge couplings leads either to excessive leakage or excessively long gate times. We show that this limitation can be overcome by two complementary protocols. The first protocol employs high-frequency SFQ pulse packets applied through the flux channel, offering a simple, analytically transparent, and robust approach for high-fidelity single-qubit control. The second protocol combines phase-shifted flux and charge pulse sequences to enhance the resonant drive and reduce the gate duration. Multilevel simulations demonstrate single-qubit gate fidelities above $99.99\%$; the simpler protocol remains robust under moderate variations of qubit parameters and flux bias, while the combined protocol preserves high fidelity while substantially accelerating the gate. These results establish SFQ-based cryogenic control as a realistic route to fast, accurate, and scalable manipulation of fluxonium qubits.

☆ Dynamical Casimir emission from Floquet-driven Landau polaritons: Gauge invariance forbids a superradiant phase transition
S. Hughes
Ultrastrong light--matter coupling of linear systems, such as Landau polaritons formed by a two-dimensional electron gas in a terahertz cavity, is described by the bosonic Hopfield model, and gauge invariance forbids a superradiant phase transition (SRPT). Modulating the magnetic field alone has been predicted to enhance the cycle-averaged coupling and induce a Floquet SRPT. We develop an exact theory of periodically driven Landau polaritons. Including the electric field induced by the modulated flux (Faraday's law), the problem reduces exactly, by Kohn's theorem, to the electronic center-of-mass mode coupled to the cavity, whose Hamiltonian is a sum of squares at every instant. A theorem of Krein then guarantees stability to all orders above a computable drive frequency, the Krein frequency, for which we give a self-contained proof. Below it, the system is stable except within resonance tongues where the drive creates pairs from the vacuum, the dynamical Casimir effect. At high drive frequency the electrons experience the mean field plus a ponderomotive trap (the Fock--Darwin problem), not an enhanced coupling. A gauge theorem excludes a Floquet photon condensate for any band structure, including Kane nonparabolicity, for which we derive a generalized Thomas--Reiche--Kuhn (TRK) sum rule. The predicted transition arises from averaging the coupling in a fixed Landau-level basis, which yields an effective model that violates the TRK sum rule; under driving, gauge invariance also requires the induced Faraday field. The rule to modulate and average the minimal-coupling Hamiltonian, not the parameters of its projection, applies to any linear, minimally coupled system. Instead of an SRPT, magnetic modulation produces dynamical Casimir emission: Faraday-driven polariton--magnetoplasmon pairs at low threshold, and two-color photon pairs with up to 5--10~dB of two-mode squeezing.
☆ A New Computational Model for the Spin-Free Sum-of-Squares Energy Bounds of Electronic Hamiltonian
Yuming Bao, Yancheng Wu, Dongdong Ge, Yinyu Ye
Optimizing spin-free sum-of-squares (SOS) energy bounds for electronic Hamiltonians leads to semidefinite programs whose expanded size grows rapidly with the orbital dimension. We derive an exact reformulation of an established spin-free SOS model as a convex quadratic problem over a single symmetric matrix constrained between zero and the identity. Explicit recovery maps connect feasible quadratic-program iterates to certificates in the original SOS formulation, and identify the Frank--Wolfe gap with the separation between recovered primal and dual objectives. We implement the quadratic action through GPU-accelerated Coulomb contractions and solve the reformulated problem using a cached implementation of fully corrective Frank--Wolfe, referred to here as the dimension-reduced simplicial method (DRSM) that caches operator products and optimizes convex-combination weights in a small corrective quadratic program. Numerical experiments cover 65 FCIDUMP models, molecular geometries, and regular hydrogen rings, including original-coordinate recovery checks on nine instances and comparisons with FISTA and a boundary-point SDP solver. On eight H100 GPUs, a cold-start calculation for C$_{720}$ with 10,080 spatial orbitals reaches a freshly recomputed Frank--Wolfe gap of $8.82\times10^{-9}$ hartree in 5.02 hours. Full-space hydrogen-ring calculations reach 10,000 orbitals, with cyclic reduction providing further computational savings. These results show how exact reformulation, data structure exploitation and reuse of Coulomb actions make optimization of the selected large-scale SOS relaxation practical.

☆ Error Resilience and Unitary 2-Designs
Zheng-Hang Sun, Fabian Ballar Trigueros, Xhek Turkeshi, Piotr Sierant
Encoding-error-decoding circuits provide a setting for studying protection of quantum information against errors. In these circuits, an encoding unitary is followed by an error layer, decoding by the inverse unitary, and ancilla postselection. For encoders drawn from unitary 2-design ensembles, these circuits exhibit an error-protecting phase below a threshold error strength in which the fidelity between the input and recovered logical states approaches unity. Here, we show how departures from Haar second-moment statistics of the encoder can destabilize the error-protecting phase and derive a universal inequality linking recovery fidelity to the second unitary frame potential, which quantifies the ensemble's proximity to a unitary 2-design. This connection is exemplified by matchgate circuits doped with a tunable number of non-Gaussian gates. We analytically show that undoped circuits lack a stable error-protecting phase in the thermodynamic limit and that increasing the doping restores the error protection mechanism as the encoder ensemble approaches an approximate unitary 2-design. Further examples of Hamiltonian encoders, including an experimentally motivated all-to-all spin model, follow the same mechanism. Our results identify recovery fidelity as a diagnostic of departures from unitary 2-design behavior in quantum many-body systems.

Jannik H. Schwarberg, Fedor D. Hrunski, Maximilian Hollendonner, Wolfgang Knolle, Mathias Rommel, Fabian J. Magerl, Jan F. Dick, Jörg Schulze

Furthermore, to address the spectral indistinguishability required for quantum networks, we precisely tune the zero-phonon line (ZPL) of individual emitters via the reverse-bias Stark effect. ☆ Edge quantum weight of finite Chern flakes and its topological floor
Rohit Narula
The zero-point energy of a circuit measures the polarization fluctuation of an insulator coupled to it. In a crystal this is the bulk quantum weight $K_\mathrm{bulk}$, which the Chern number $C$ bounds below by $|C|$. We show that a finite Chern flake adds an edge term that survives as the flake grows. The low-frequency transitions of its chiral edge carry a dipole weight, the sum of their squared dipole matrix elements, $K_\mathrm{edge}\geq|C|$ per unit area, a floor that follows from the positive absorption of both circular polarizations by every transition and the known cancellation of circular dichroism between edge and bulk. A weakly coupled circuit slower than the edge modes therefore reads $K_\mathrm{bulk}+K_\mathrm{edge}$, averaged over two field directions, while a faster one below the bulk gap approaches $K_\mathrm{bulk}$, so which quantum weight is measured depends on whether the flake is made large or the circuit slow first. Exact free-fermion calculations on lattice flakes bear out the floor and this dependence on the circuit frequency. The result holds at weak coupling, which a growing flake at fixed coupling eventually leaves. Above the floor, the edge weight of one channel is a number fixed by the shape of the boundary and the edge velocities, which square and rectangular lattice flakes follow to within 0.003. Each further edge channel adds its own such number, while the circular dichroism of the edge counts only the net chirality.

☆ Classical phase unwrapping enables large-time-step unitary quantum Krylov subspace diagonalization
Tushar Kumar Jain, Rahul Maitra, Nicholas J. Mayhall
For computing molecular energies on early fault-tolerant hardware, unitary quantum Krylov subspace diagonalization (UQKSD) avoids both the deep circuits of quantum phase estimation and the Pauli-term sampling of variational methods by extracting the energies from a projected real-time propagator. At a small time step $τ$, nearly linearly dependent Krylov vectors make the overlap matrix ill-conditioned. Our tests at fixed total evolution time show that additional Krylov vectors then add no accuracy, while the thresholded energy becomes increasingly sensitive to the choice of cutoff. A larger time step improves the conditioning and reduces the Krylov dimension $M$ needed for a target accuracy, but the energies are then known only modulo $2π/τ$. We present Classical Unwrapping for Resolving Eigenvalues (CURE-QKSD), a classical post-processing method that leaves the UQKSD circuits and generalized eigenvalue problem unchanged and recovers the missing multiples of $2π/τ$ from phase-consistency landscapes of one or, when needed, two UQKSD runs. In noiseless tests on six molecules with 12--20 qubits, all 28 targeted energies are recovered in their aliased regimes with final errors of at most $1.1\times10^{-7}$~Ha. Under Gaussian noise with $σ=10^{-4}$, the median error of the ground or first excited state reaches chemical accuracy at large aliased time steps with $M=20$--$65$, whereas uncorrected principal-branch energies are off by $0.7$--$115$~Ha. CURE-QKSD therefore makes aliased time steps usable for UQKSD calculations with smaller, better-conditioned Krylov bases.
☆ Disorder-Induced Logarithmic Spreading and Localization of Quantum Fluctuations
Ang Yang, Jingxuan Zhang, Lei Ying
Disorder can localize quantum particles, even in the presence of interactions, but its influence on quantum fluctuations beyond mean--field dynamics remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate the propagation of quantum fluctuations in weakly interacting disordered bosonic systems by comparing the Bose--Hubbard model with the Gross--Pitaevskii equation. We find that, in contrast to ballistic spreading in the disorder--free system, quantum fluctuations exhibit logarithmic spreading at intermediate times under both random and quasiperiodic disorder, before eventually saturating. The spreading rate decreases algebraically with increasing disorder strength, and this behavior persists across different particle numbers and extends to two dimensions. Using a time--dependent Bogoliubov--de Gennes framework, we identify the localized mean--field wavefunction as a time--dependent pairing background that generates quantum fluctuations. The exponential suppression of fluctuation--generation rates with distance provides a physical mechanism for the logarithmically advancing fluctuation front. Our results reveal a distinct regime of disorder--controlled quantum--fluctuation dynamics and establish disorder as a means of controlling their spreading.

We prove a nonasymptotic electric-flux truncation bound for the entire vacuum-relative low-energy window of the original pure compact $U(1)$ lattice Hamiltonian. On a three-dimensional periodic cubic lattice with $N\geq3$ sites per direction at $θ=0$, in the gauge-invariant zero-global-flux sector, the factorial-squared tail-norm estimate holds for every normalized vector in the window, without physical eigenvalue-isolation, window-edge gap, or nondegeneracy assumptions and without a window-dimension factor. In this regime, the coherent part of the electric dipole-dipole interaction is larger than the dissipative part, and a single photon emission can transfer large momenta (larger than ten times the single photon recoil) to the atoms. For off-resonant laser light, the atoms are dressed with an electric dipole moment of $\approx$ 1 Debye and interact coherently. This light-induced dipole-dipole interaction has been previously observed only in the far-field mean-field regime. For two atoms, the resonance is shifted by the two-body Lamb shift which is dominated by the near-field part of the dipolar interaction. Dipolar resonance shifts have been observed before only for many atoms interacting with the far-field part of the dipolar interaction. Our work sheds new light on photoassociation processes and paves the way for studying driven quantum systems with strong electric dipole-dipole interactions.

Existing QLS algorithms have runtimes that scale linearly with the condition number $κ(A)$, the sparsity of $A$, and logarithmically with inverse precision, but often overlook structural properties of $\vec{b}$, whose alignment with $A$'s eigenspaces can greatly affect performance. In this work, we present a new QLS algorithm that explicitly leverages the structure of the right-hand side vector $\vec{b}$. The runtime of our algorithm depends polynomially on the sparsity of the augmented matrix $H = [A, -\vec{b}]$, the inverse precision, the $\ell_2$ norm of the solution $\vec{y} = A^+ \vec{b}$, and a new instance-dependent parameter \[ ET= \sum_{i=1}^M p_i^2 \cdot d_i, \] where $\vec{p} = (AA^{\top})^+ \vec{b}$, and $d_i$ denotes the squared $\ell_2$ norm of the $i$-th row of $H$. We also introduce a structure-aware rescaling technique tailored to the solution $\vec{y} = A^+ \vec{b}$. Unlike left preconditioning methods, which transform the linear system to $DA\vec{y} = D\vec{b}$, our approach applies a right rescaling matrix, reformulating the linear system as $AD\vec{z} = \vec{b}$. As an application of our instance-aware QLS algorithm and new rescaling scheme, we develop a quantum algorithm for solving multivariate polynomial systems in regimes where prior QLS-based methods fail. This yields an end-to-end framework applicable to a broad class of problems. In particular, we apply it to the maximum independent set (MIS) problem, formulated as a special case of a polynomial system, and show through detailed analysis that, under certain conditions, our quantum algorithm for MIS runs in polynomial time.

Here, $\mathsf{UQMA}$ is the unique witness version of $\mathsf{QMA}$, and $\mathsf{UQMA} \cap \mathsf{co}$-$\mathsf{UQMA}$ precisely captures the complexity of BPE without the known guiding state. Remarkably, this problem is, to our knowledge, the first natural problem complete for $\mathsf{UQMA} \cap \mathsf{co}$-$\mathsf{UQMA}$. These results advance the role of quantum computing in the study of topological phases of matter and provide a pathway for clarifying the connection between topological phases of matter and computational complexity.

♻ ☆ Entanglement and magic transitions in an all-to-all non-Hermitian spin model
Sasanka Dowarah, Michael Kolodrubetz
The long-time state of a non-Hermitian system is determined by the eigenvalue with the largest imaginary part. In interacting many-body systems this eigenvalue usually cannot be tracked analytically, and the character of the state it selects is unknown. We construct a non-Hermitian spin ensemble of $L$ spins with exactly $k$-local all-to-all interactions, in which this dominant eigenvalue can be tracked analytically from the clean limit into the disordered regime. Disorder produces a competition between an isolated spectral outlier and the edge of a many-body spectral bulk. We study three cases: purely anti-Hermitian disorder, purely Hermitian disorder, and mixed disorder of equal strength. For purely anti-Hermitian and mixed disorder, we show that when the bulk overtakes the outlier in imaginary part, the dominant eigenstate switches from an outlier state with low entanglement and magic (nonstabilizerness) to a bulk state with substantially larger entanglement and magic, with both changing at the same threshold. For $k \gg \sqrt{L}$ the bulk has a sharp spectral edge and the transition thresholds follow in closed form, while for $k \ll \sqrt{L}$ spectral tails broaden the transition into a crossover. Purely Hermitian disorder provides a contrasting case with no outlier-to-bulk switching. Finally, we map the non-Hermitian evolution exactly onto postselected trajectories of a monitored quantum system, connecting this spectral mechanism to measurement-induced transitions.

♻ ☆ Nonunitary Quantum Criticality Driven by a General Boundary Condition: Exact Solution
Yao Zhou, Peng Ye
Nonunitary quantum critical phenomena remain largely unexplored, hindered by the scarcity of exactly solvable models and the numerical challenges in non-Hermitian systems. Here we demonstrate that a general boundary condition drives fundamentally new nonunitary boundary quantum criticality in an exactly solvable lattice model. The exact solution yields a closed-form expression for the boundary-induced equal-time correlation function. The algebraic long-distance behavior of the boundary-induced correlation is governed by the single-particle reflection amplitude at the Fermi level, whose anomalous amplification is forbidden in unitary scattering and therefore provides a direct scattering signature of the nonunitary boundary-critical regime. We use the biorthogonal entanglement entropy as a many-body probe of this boundary-critical behavior and find that it retains logarithmic scaling, while the associated effective central charge, continuously tunable by the boundary parameters, changes from real to complex. The real branch admits a unitary defect conformal field theory (CFT) description, whereas the complex branch lies beyond analytic continuation from the unitary theory. These results establish minimal boundary engineering as an exactly solvable platform for nonunitary boundary quantum criticality and provide a benchmark for broader studies of nonunitary critical phenomena.

We further prepare a one-flux-added quasihole and characterize its fractional charge response against finite-size benchmarks. ♻ ☆ Parallel and Distributed Fermionic Simulation via Dynamic Encoding
Michael Williams de la Bastida, Peter V. Coveney
We demonstrate a simple and efficient method to parallelize and distribute Trotterized Hamiltonian simulation of fermionic systems across multiple QPUs. Using combinatorial covering designs to define a fixed set of fermion-qubit encodings, independent of system size, we demonstrate communication cost scaling as $\mathcal{O}(M q^3 r)$ for a system of $M$ fermionic modes and Trotter number $r$. This improves on the static encoding bound for $q$ QPUs, $\mathcal{O}(M^4 q r)$. In terms of QPU register size $R$, at most $R^{1/3}$ QPUs are able to parallelize at most $R^{4/3}$ fermionic modes. We compare this approach to dynamic encoding using a randomized method, Pauli-weight based optimization and hypergraph partitioning. Applying these to the Hamiltonians of a range of molecular systems split across two and three QPUs, we find the combinatorial covering approach results in significantly reduced communication cost.

♻ ☆ Semi-device-independent channel identification with communication matrices
Samgeeth Puliyil, Leevi Leppäjärvi, Mário Ziman
We look into the task of differentiating between any two quantum channels and reconstructing them from the obtained measurement statistics with possibly limited information about the experimental set-up. We employ the communication matrix formalism where the measurement statistics of a prepare-and-measure scenario is represented as a stochastic communication matrix. In order to differentiate between any two quantum channels, the informational completeness of the set-up is both necessary and sufficient. On the other hand, if we want to uniquely characterize any quantum channel, in addition we also need to have a complete description of the set-up. We show that in many important cases we can deduce this information directly from the communication matrix of the set-up before applying the channel. Given that we trust the dimension of the system, we show that we can deduce the information completeness of the set-up directly from the rank of the communication matrix. Furthermore, we show that another quantity of the communication matrix, called the information storability, can be used to self-test the set-up (up to an orthogonal transformation) for an important class of states and measurements. This provides us a semi-device-independent way to identify quantum channels from the prepare-and-measure statistics. Lastly, we consider scenarios where we might have some additional information about the channels or additional resources at our disposal which could help us relax some of the assumptions of the proposed scenario.

♻ ☆ Tunable quantum Mpemba effect in long-range interacting systems
Andrew Hallam, Matthew Yusuf, Aashish A. Clerk, Ivar Martin, Zlatko Papić
Symmetry plays a fundamental role in many-body systems, both in and out of equilibrium. The quantum Mpemba effect (QME) -- a phenomenon where systems initially farther from equilibrium can thermalize faster -- can be understood in terms of how rapidly a symmetry, broken by initial conditions, is dynamically restored. In this work, we study the QME in a one-dimensional spin-1/2 XYZ model with power-law decaying interactions in the presence of a magnetic field. In the prethermal regime generated by large field strengths, the system develops a continuous U(1) symmetry, enabling the QME to emerge. However, due to the Hohenberg-Mermin-Wagner theorem, the QME can only arise when interactions are sufficiently short-ranged. This leads to an interplay between the external field, interaction range, and dynamical symmetry restoration. We systematically explore this interplay and analyze the dependence of the QME on the effective temperature set by the initial state. Our results demonstrate the tunability of the QME via long-range interactions, which can be probed in experimental platforms of trapped ions, polar molecules, and NV centers.

♻ ☆ Fulqrum: a generalized framework for quantum subspace diagonalization
Paul D. Nation, Abdullah Ash Saki, Hwajung Kang
We present an open-source software framework for computing the solution to Hamiltonian eigenproblems in a subspace defined by bit-strings sampled from a quantum computer. Hamiltonians are represented using an extended alphabet that includes projection and ladder operators, yielding a unified solution method for qubit and fermionic systems. Operators are grouped and sorted so that only non-zero terms need be evaluated and a minimal number of subspace lookup operations performed. Bit-strings are expressed using bit-sets to reduce memory consumption and allow for evaluating operators with no fundamental limit on the number of qubits. Subspaces defined over bit-sets are stored in a hash map format that allows for efficient indexing and lookup operations. Specializations for problems, such as those from quantum chemistry, can further reduce computational costs. Our method can be used to directly construct sparse matrix Hamiltonian representations or obtain matrix-free solutions, allowing users to utilize their eigensolver of choice. We show the benefits of our framework by computing the ground-state solution to examples from condensed matter physics and quantum chemistry with less memory and runtime compared to existing techniques, in some cases by two orders of magnitude or more. This work provides a flexible interface for performant quantum-classical eigensolutions for candidate quantum advantage applications.

♻ ☆ Divergence between Maximum-Probability and Maximum-Likelihood Decoding in the Low-Noise Limit of Quantum Error Correction
Yixin Zhao, Fei Yan
In the asymptotic low-noise limit of quantum error correction, two optimal decoding rules can disagree. Maximum-probability (MP) decoding selects the most probable microscopic error, whereas degenerate maximum-likelihood (MLD) decoding selects the logical sector with the largest total probability. Under code-capacity Pauli noise, we determine the first physical error weight $m$ at which the MP and MLD logical winner sets become provably disjoint, even under optimal MP tie resolution. As the physical error rate tends to zero, MLD retains a residual zero-temperature degeneracy from the multiplicity of minimum-weight errors sharing a syndrome and logical label, which can outweigh the single most probable error. Code distance imposes the universal bound $m\geq h=\lceil d/2\rceil$; the rigidity depth $r$, defined by $m=h+r$, counts the additional error-weight shells above $h$ on which MP and MLD remain equivalent. We certify a three-level hierarchy: $r=0$ for planar surface codes and two recursively concatenated families, $r=1$ for odd-distance square toric codes and the Gross $[[144,12,12]]$ quantum low-density-parity-check code, and $r=2$ for a separable family with hypergraph product and bivariate bicycle descriptions. The onset weight fixes the leading failure-rate gap between best-tie MP and MLD, proportional to the $m$th power of the physical noise strength, providing an exact subthreshold benchmark for the advantage of degeneracy-aware decoding over the computationally cheaper nondegenerate rule.
♻ ☆ Accelerated spin-adapted ground-state preparation with nonvariational quantum algorithms
Takumi Kobori, Taichi Kosugi, Hirofumi Nishi, Synge Todo, Yu-ichiro Matsushita
Various methods have been explored to prepare the spin-adapted ground state, the lowest energy state within the Hilbert space constrained by externally specified values of the total spin magnitude and the spin-$z$ component. In such problem settings, nonvariational methods incorporate penalty terms into the original Hamiltonian to enforce the desired constraints. Such additional terms would require a quartic number of gates in terms of the number $n_{\textrm{spin}}$ of spins when naively implemented. To circumvent this computationally intensive scaling, this paper proposes a new nonvariational procedure to obtain the spin-adapted ground states that requires only quadratic scaling. The proposed method consists of two stages: the first stage is to prepare a spin-magnitude adapted state and the second stage is post-processing for the desired $S_z$. By separating into two stages, the procedure achieves the desired spin-adapted ground state while reducing the number of penalty terms from $O(n_{\textrm{spin}}^4)$ to $O(n_{\textrm{spin}}^2)$. We conducted numerical experiments for spin-1/2 Heisenberg ring models and manganese trimer systems. The results confirmed the effectiveness of our method, demonstrating a significant reduction in gate complexity and validating its practical usefulness.

♻ ☆ Millisecond optical coherence and strong collective coupling in an integrated telecom rare-earth photonic platform
Kah Jen Wo, Pavel A. Dmitriev, Karthik Dasigi, Fumiya Hanamura, Steven Touzard
Long-range quantum network nodes require the combination of strong light-matter coupling, long coherence times and in-situ spectral control at telecom wavelengths. The coherence of erbium in integrated devices is held back by its hosts, which do not simultaneously provide the weakly magnetic nuclear-spin environment and the well-defined substitutional sites found in coherence-optimised bulk crystals. Here we bring such an optimised crystal onto a photonic chip, by bonding an Er${^{3+}}$:CaWO${_{4}}$ host without an adhesive interlayer to a high-${Q}$ electro-optically tuneable thin-film lithium niobate microring resonator. At an effective temperature of 75mK and a field of only 0.2T, ions probed through a waveguide show an effective homogeneous linewidth of ${289\pm5}$Hz (${T_{\text{M}}=1.10\pm0.02}$ms), with spectral diffusion proceeding at ${86\pm18}$Hz and saturating at ${1.5\pm0.2}$kHz. Electro-optically tuning the resonator through the erbium optical transition resolves an avoided crossing with a collective cooperativity of ${C=6.7\pm0.4}$ at zero field and ${C=4.9\pm0.2}$ at 0.4T, where ${T_{\text{M}}}$ exceeds 1ms. Exploiting superhyperfine coupling to the host's ${^{183}}$W nuclear spins, we store and retrieve optical phase information over 5s with a visibility of ${0.935\pm0.015}$. Strong collective coupling, millisecond coherence and in-situ spectral tuning in a single device thus establish heterogeneous integration leveraging coherence-optimised hosts as a route to scalable telecom quantum networks.
♻ ☆ Quantum Simulation of Quantum Channels and Applications
Lúcio S. Fassarella
We review the basic theory of quantum channels and develop a strategy for simulating them on digital quantum computers, drawing upon the Choi-Kraus operator-sum representation and Stinespring dilation to provide a unified approach for various applications. We discuss three types of applications, offering explicit examples for each: the preparation of mixed states, measurements described by positive operator-valued measures (POVMs), and the simulation of the evolution of Markovian quantum systems. We recover fundamental concepts from quantum theory, such as the purification of a mixed state and the Naimark dilation associated with a POVM. Regarding the simulation of the evolution of a Markovian quantum system, we introduce an operator, termed the residual operator, to construct, from the system's Liouvillian, a quantum channel that serves as a first-order approximation of the quantum dynamical semigroup. This allows the simulation of quantum dynamics to be performed in a manner analogous to the Euler method for ordinary differential equations, avoiding Trotterization. We prove all the theoretical results mentioned, with the exception of the fundamental Choi-Kraus theorem concerning the operator-sum representation of quantum channels, for which we provide the appropriate references. The explicit simulations discussed were implemented using the AerSimulator from IBM's Qiskit SDK, with the corresponding code available on GitHub.

♻ ☆ Single-molecule strong optomechanical regimes in SERS via hybrid plasmonic cavities
Miguel Á. Martínez-García, Johannes Feist, Diego Martín-Cano
We identify enhanced strong coherent Surface-Enhanced Raman Scattering (SERS) interactions facilitated by hybridized metallo-dielectric cavities with a resonant fluorescent molecule. By illuminating a detuned electronic transition near saturation via a narrowband hybrid plasmonic mode, we observe enhanced splittings in the Stokes and anti-Stokes spectra, revealing strong optomechanical coupling and nonlinear vibrational modifications at intensities far below irreversible SERS damage thresholds. We compute the second-order photon correlations that allows identifying the nonclassical character associated to these strong optomechanical interactions and SERS configurations that enables them to optically characterize the anharmonic character of the vibrational modes.
♻ ☆ How many degrees of freedom describe a quantum N-particle state?
Matthew J. Lake, Marek L. Miller
In Newtonian spacetime, the canonical description of a classical $N$-particle system requires $3N$ degrees of freedom. Not all of these are physical, however, since the conservation of the net momentum implies that only $3(N-1)$ accelerations are independent. Hence, three constraints can be used to eliminate the unphysical centre-of-mass variables, at the level of the Lagrangian, leaving only the subset of observable displacements and momenta, which are relational. Imposing the constraints does not change the dynamics of these variables, at the classical level, and is analogous to a gauge-fixing procedure, which removes redundancy in the description of the system. In classical physics, therefore, the number of physical degrees of freedom equals the number of independent relational degrees of freedom. Here, we show that this is not the case in quantum mechanics. While an operator-analogue of the classical net momentum exists, it cannot be used to impose constraints that restrict the degrees of freedom in the theory, without a loss of physical information. This means that all $3N$ canonical degrees of freedom are physical, even though only $3(N-1)$ of them are relational. We explore the physical consequences of the non-relational variables and show that they give rise to generalised uncertainty relations (GURs), for the relational quantities that define the quantum reference frame (QRF). Hence, it is shown that the non-relational degrees of freedom refer to the frame itself and that the non-Heisenberg terms in the GURs define its Galilean-invariant spreads, in both real space and momentum space. The implications of this result for recent work on relational models, including the ``perspective neutral'' framework for QRFs, are discussed. Its implications for the wider relational program, and, in particular, the relevance of the latter to quantum gravity research, are also critically assessed

♻ ☆ CV-QKD over Turbulence Channels with Virtual Photon Subtraction and Quantum Multiple-Symbol Detection for Underwater Quantum Communications

Continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CV-QKD) is a promising approach for secure underwater quantum communications (UQCs), where propagation loss, scattering, turbulence, and receiver thermal noise can severely degrade the transmission of quantum states. In this paper, we propose an underwater CV-QKD system with virtual photon subtraction (VPS), implemented through post-selection of Alice's measurement outcomes, without requiring channel state information (CSI) at the receiver. Three VPS-based system configurations are analyzed, corresponding to homodyne detection (VPS-HD), quantum maximum-likelihood detection (VPS-QMLD), and quantum multiple-symbol detection (VPS-QMSD). System performance is evaluated in terms of the accepted-only quantum bit error rate (QBER), where underwater turbulence is modeled by an Erlang distribution. Analytical and semi-closed-form QBER expressions are derived for the three configurations and validated through Monte Carlo simulations for different water types and system parameters. The results show close agreement between analytical and simulation results and demonstrate that VPS-QMSD provides the best robustness against underwater turbulence, achieving the lowest QBER compared with VPS-QMLD and VPS-HD.
♻ ☆ Programmable quantum simulation of anharmonic dynamics

♻ ☆ Causal Order Cannot Be An Observable
Declan Maguire, Fabio Costa
Recent developments in the formalisation of quantum causal structures have made it possible to test and compare hypotheses about causal structure empirically, rather than being a-priori assumptions. Such differences in causal structure may be leveraged to distinguish between the processes they belong to, akin to distinguishing between quantum states known to belong to different eigenspaces of an observable. So how far this analogy can be pushed? Can causal order be interpreted as a kind of observable? Can it be measured? To this end we construct a completely operational definition of observables in terms of `discrimination tasks'. This begins with some base set of classes (analogous to a quantum observable's eigenspaces) before we impose three conditions on how these classes relate under discrimination tasks. These conditions recover the properties of a standard observable, letting us apply this definition to non-state entities such as quantum processes, which naturally encode causal structure. The first of these conditions (1) asserts that a member of any class is perfectly distinguishable from a member of any other class -- for states, this implies conditions (2) and (3), but we show this does not hold automatically for processes (or indeed channels). By analysing classes of quantum processes having strict causal orders, we find causal classes which are sharp but violate condition 2 (but not 3), and classes which are likewise sharp and violate condition 3 (but not 2). This implies that causal order cannot be an observable.

♻ ☆ QuantumBilliards.jl: An extensible, user friendly, high-performance Julia library for the large scale computation of spectra and eigenstates of quantum billiards and related problems

We present QuantumBilliards.jl, an open-source Julia library providing a suite of numerical solvers for the two-dimensional interior Helmholtz eigenproblem with Dirichlet boundary conditions, a paradigmatic model in quantum chaos. The library implements conventional wavenumber-sweep techniques together with several accelerated eigensolvers: the Vergini--Saraceno scaling method, the expanded boundary integral method (EBIM), Beyn's contour-integral method, and the Compact Rational Krylov (CORK) method. It provides a common framework for constructing billiard geometries, exploiting discrete symmetries, computing eigenvalues and eigenstates, and treating smooth, cornered, and multiply connected domains. The library further includes reconstruction of eigenfunctions from boundary normal derivatives and the computation of Poincaré--Husimi (PH) phase-space representations. Available at: https://github.com/Quantum-Chaos-Julia/QuantumBilliards.jl.

♻ ☆ Raman anyon-Hubbard model in a 1D Bose lattice gas
Josep Cabedo, Claudio Iacovelli, Leticia Tarruell, Alessio Celi
The anyon-Hubbard model is the paradigmatic lattice model of one-dimensional (1D) anyons, in which chiral interactions make bosons equivalent to particles with fractional statistics. Its continuum limit, the chiral BF theory, emerges as the low-energy description of a Raman-coupled Bose gas with imbalanced interactions. Here, we show that loading such a gas into a 1D optical lattice realizes the lattice counterpart of this theory, which we name the Raman anyon-Hubbard model. The Raman-dressed bosons acquire density-dependent Peierls phases when tunneling through occupied sites. For a small statistical phase, the model reduces to the anyon-Hubbard model, while beyond this limit it defines a distinct lattice anyon model with unbounded rather than periodic statistical interactions. Numerically, we show that the dressed gas displays the defining properties of 1D anyons, namely a density-dependent asymmetry of the ground-state momentum distribution, interaction-induced asymmetric transport and chiral bound states. Remarkably, these features are readily accessible with Raman-coupled $^{39}$K atoms, opening up the experimental exploration of 1D anyons beyond the few-particle regime.

♻ ☆ Are quantum measurements universal?
Massimiliano Sassoli de Bianchi
In 2014, with D. Aerts, we showed, in the extended Bloch representation of quantum mechanics, that the Born rule results from a universal average over all the ways the measurement-interaction can be selected, computed by averaging over discretized (cellular) densities and taking a continuum limit. N. Shackel has since criticized this construction, in the context of Bertrand's paradox, for depending on the discretization adopted, for the constancy of its averages, and for the unclear sense in which the average is over 'all' densities. His criticisms prompt the present re-examination. What makes a random way of selecting a measurement 'universal', we argue, is that it privileges no portion of the structure of the available interactions, a property we call indifference and adopt as definitional. We prove that every universal measurement, however constructed, produces exactly the Born probabilities: the universal average is unique, the 2014 construction is one realization among infinitely many, and for cellular measurements the result is exact at every finite resolution, with no limit to be taken, which explains the constancy of the averages. Non-trivial universal measurements exist, but must involve deterministic measurements: Dirichlet processes are universal measurements whose support contains every way of selecting an interaction, whereas one free of deterministic components selects the uniform density, so that for it the Born rule holds with certainty, not merely on average. In sequences of measurements, deterministic components produce deviations from quantum statistics governed by a single parameter, in principle accessible to experiment. The only geometric input is the Euclidean length of the membrane and the orthogonal landing of the point-particle, where Gleason's theorem enters. We indicate the generalization to any number of outcomes and the bearing on Bertrand's paradox.

In finite-dimensional quantum systems, such as the Lipkin--Meshkov--Glick (LMG) model and the mixed-field Ising model at the chaotic point, we provide numerical evidence that logK-complexity discriminates between genuine and saddle-dominated scrambling at early times, correctly avoiding the exponential contribution coming from the unstable saddle in the former case, and closely tracking the conventional Krylov complexity in the latter. We supplement these analyses by extending the Krylov formalism in classical dynamical systems and defining classical versions of these operator growth measures, showing that the false positives arising from unstable saddles in classical phase space are non-existent.

♻ ☆ Imaging spin entanglement with a scanning tunneling microscope

The zeroth moment probes the one-tangle in systems with a gapped, nondegenerate ground state. For rotationally invariant Heisenberg systems, the first moment yields thermal spin correlators $\langle\boldsymbol S(i)\cdot\boldsymbol S(j)\rangle$, enabling reconstruction of nearest-neighbor concurrence and spatial imaging of entanglement in spin chains. It also provides access to the internal energy and magnetic specific heat, both usable as entanglement witnesses. Applying this approach to experimental IETS data from nanographene spin chains, we find good agreement with theory. We further discuss how the second moment probes longer-range correlations and the inverse moment relates to local spin susceptibility. For spin-$1/2$ trimers, we connect inter-multiplet inelastic spectral weight to genuine tripartite entanglement quantified by the concurrence fill. Finally, we reconcile the local character of IETS with its sensitivity to nonlocal entanglement through an analogy with digital quantum circuits, where Hamiltonian evolution implements multiqubit operations. These results establish IETS as a tool for quantifying and imaging entanglement in engineered on-surface spin systems.

Non-Hermitian topological systems have attracted a lot of research activities in recent times, both theoretically and experimentally, due to their unique physical properties and association with open quantum systems. We show that modular structures, where specific couplings at regular intervals take distinct values, enrich the unique topological attributes of these systems such as the non-Hermitian skin effect and the breakdown of conventional bulk-boundary correspondence. These systems also possess the capability of displaying criticality-enhanced sensitivity for precision metrology. We establish how the modular structure, in suitable parameter regime, enhances their sensing performance near spectral topological phase transitions and show that the enhancement can be achieved in multi-parameter estimation scenarios as well.

♻ ☆ Interaction-driven Weyl superfluids from topologically trivial bands in an optical Raman lattice

We propose an interaction-driven route to Weyl superfluidity from topologically trivial noninteracting bands in a three-dimensional optical Raman lattice. The scheme builds on a pairing mechanism arising from the interplay between a large Zeeman splitting and an attractive Hubbard interaction. The large Zeeman splitting renders the noninteracting bands topologically trivial and suppresses spin-flip hopping. These otherwise off-resonant spin-flip processes are resonantly restored when the attractive Hubbard interaction compensates the energy mismatch, generating occupation-dependent spin-orbit coupling that coherently couples neighboring spin-down fermion pairs to onsite doublons. Combining this density-dependent in-plane spin-orbit coupling with density-dependent spin-conserving interlayer tunneling extends the pairing mechanism to three dimensions. A self-consistent mean-field treatment of the microscopic model yields Weyl superfluids with two, four, or eight nodes, together with fully gapped weak topological superfluids. Tuning the interaction strength and particle filling drives transitions between these phases and controls the number of Weyl nodes. We further propose an experimental implementation with ultracold ${}^{40}\mathrm{K}$ atoms. Our results provide a route to Weyl superfluidity enabled by interaction-assisted spin-orbit coupling, without requiring nontrivial single-particle band topology.

Using a known coherence bound, we determine the complete pure-state readout interval at fixed target-character fidelity. Discarding the response leaves a mixture of phase-oracle channels whose distance from the target, measured by half the diamond norm, is at most the target-character infidelity, with equality for surjective functions. We then identify when coherence alone determines performance and when apparatus correlations or loss profiles are also needed. For coherent analyzer errors, we derive the full quadratic loss and an exact scalar reduction of the profile model on the upper phase--value boundary. For mode-dependent loss, no-detection events can carry value information, and a universal bound is attained under a phase--loss compatibility condition. Photonic-mesh simulations test the analyzer-error predictions, with the controlled oracle itself assumed. Selected results extend to finite non-Abelian groups, where scalar phase kickback is restricted to one-dimensional representations.

♻ ☆ Pauli-Z Moment Matrices in the Variational Quantum Power Method: Goemans-Williamson Rounding, Qubit Locking, and a Correlation-Based Circuit-Cutting Heuristic

The matrix of single- and two-qubit Pauli-Z expectation values of any quantum state is the moment matrix of its computational-basis outcome distribution; it therefore lies in the cut polytope and, in particular, is a feasible point of the degree-2 Sum-of-Squares (Goemans-Williamson, GW) relaxation. Applying GW random-hyperplane rounding to this matrix yields cuts of expected weight at least alpha_GW times the state's energy. This observation and the resulting bound are not new: the bound is the GW inequality applied to the circuit's covariance matrix, and it was stated and used in exactly this form by Martinez, Fawzi and Stilck Franca, who interpret it as showing that a classical surrogate nearly reproduces the circuit and add noisy-circuit guarantees and hardware experiments; relax-and-round of QAOA correlation matrices, with spectral rather than hyperplane rounding, was introduced earlier by Dupont and Sundar. The bound is also not stronger than what direct computational-basis sampling of the state already gives in expectation. In this note we revisit the bound as a post-processing of the two-point data produced by variational algorithms such as QAOA and the Variational Quantum Power Method (VQPM), and give an energy-leakage bound for VQPM qubit locking. We further discuss a heuristic that uses the connected Z-correlation matrix to propose candidate qubit bipartitions for circuit cutting, in the spirit of existing correlation- and mutual-information-based partitioning methods, together with product-state error bounds in terms of quantum mutual information. Pairwise Z-correlations neither certify product structure of the state nor factorization of the underlying unitary, and the error bounds require quantities not available from Z-data alone.

♻ ☆ Reading Why: Born-Measured Attention with Exact Word Evidence on Light and Qubits

We build a transformer in which every nonlinearity is a quadratic detection (an interference, a balanced interferometric reading or a camera) and the output is a Born probability: attention $|\langle q|k\rangle|^2$, the form of the Born rule, normalised over each row, a measured product in place of the feed-forward nonlinearity, and a Born readout; between detections a classical controller squares, divides, rescales and re-encodes. With its denominators held at their values for the input, each class probability is a polynomial in the word amplitudes, so its integrated-gradient evidence is computed by a finite quadrature with no quadrature error: the words' contributions sum to the class probability above its no-information share, to $10^{-13}$ or better. On e-SNLI natural language inference the model reaches 77.45 +- 0.91 % test accuracy, level within the spread of three seeds with a softmax transformer of the same size (76.62 +- 0.36 %). Deleting the word its evidence ranks first changes the answer in 44 % of test pairs, out of the 53 % any single deletion can change, against 32 % for the softmax model's integrated gradients and 31 % for the Born Transformer's own attention. The same weights compile exactly to optoelectronic optics (simulated), and its attention overlaps to Hadamard tests on qubits; a separate coherent attention layer becomes one post-selected circuit (852 CNOTs on 23 qubits). On IBM's ibm_kingston, reading only the attention overlaps, the device gave the model's answers on the two shortest test pairs, also when the one word that decides one of them was deleted; with calibration circuits as deep as the overlaps, each word's evidence with the device's attention row sums followed the exact evidence on one pair (correlation 0.997) and on the other less closely (0.962).

We also show that it grows at most polynomially for involutive dual-unitary Yang--Baxter gates and for arbitrary phase dressings of permutation gates obtained from non-degenerate Yang--Baxter maps. These results imply, respectively, constant and logarithmic upper bounds on the operator entanglement. Conversely, we construct a seven-state involutive Yang--Baxter gate without dual unitarity and a one-site operator whose exact operator Schmidt rank grows exponentially, although the corresponding operator entropies remain undetermined. Entanglement growth in the general Yang--Baxter case remains open. All proofs and selected examples were constructed by ChatGPT.

We investigate what can still be learned from the dynamics in a dephased Bose--Marletto--Vedral setup. The distinction survives, with a modified sensitivity, when the comparison is enlarged to population-preserving classical measurement and feedback through a diagonal PPT relaxation. The answer is set by the field. In a field along [111], three quarters of the bath centres lie off the field axis, and the moment of their $m_s = 0$ state along the field grows from 0.04 at 25 G to 0.46 at 300 G and 0.81 at 800 G. At 25 G the polarized bath is therefore nearly silent: at 0.57 ppm the dephasing time $T_2^*$ of a separately addressed $^{15}$NV$^-$ probe is 112 $μ$s, six times the 18.0 $μ$s of a P1 bath, and still 2.4 times at 90% polarization; an ensemble measurement gains a factor of two. At 300 G the advantage over P1 shrinks to 1.4, and at 800 G the polarized bath dephases faster than P1. The field dependence of every bath, P1 included, follows the mean moment of its centres along the field. For the Hahn echo, bath relaxation ($T_1$ = 6 ms) caps the gain: a $^{15}$NV$^-$ probe in a polarized bath reaches 1.5 times the P1 value at 25 G and 1.14-1.16 times at 300 and 800 G. This excess was recently attributed to additional dark defects. We show that the excess comes mostly from the frozen field. In our model the P1 centres outside each cluster flip-flop in pairs: two centres exchange their spin states and conserve their total $S_z$. Kinetic Monte Carlo generates these events at golden-rule rates, which follow from the dipolar Hamiltonian without adjustable parameters, and each cluster evolves in the resulting time-dependent field. This dynamical mean field lies between the static-mean-field and mean-field-free limits. For a $^{14}$N P1 bath it reduces $T_2\cdot$[N] at 30 mT from 264 $\pm$ 16 to 188 $\pm$ 12 $μ$s ppm and gives 167 $\pm$ 11 $μ$s ppm at 10 mT, 1.7 and 0.4 standard deviations from experiment, with no dark spins. When each centre jumps independently, $T_2\cdot$[N] is 147 $\pm$ 9 $μ$s ppm at 30 mT; the correlation of the flip-flop partners thus lengthens $T_2$ by 20-30 percent at high field. The Overhauser field is neither frozen nor averaged out by fast motion: 68-83 percent of its autocorrelation survives 200 $μ$s. At 2.5 mT, where the P1 electron and nucleus hybridise, $T_2$ stays below experiment for any choice of rates. Part of the field dependence therefore remains: $T_2$ rises by a factor 1.69 $\pm$ 0.07 instead of 2.15 $\pm$ 0.08 from 2.5 to 30 mT.
♻ ☆ Theoretical study of nitrogen-vacancy spin coherence enhanced by vacancy aggregation in diamond using cluster-correlation expansion
Chikara Shinei
Annealing a semiconductor makes its vacancies mobile; they aggregate into multi-vacancy complexes that often carry spin. Such centres are a magnetic-noise source for any spin qubit among them, in silicon and silicon carbide as well as in diamond, and they are accordingly blamed for the decoherence of negatively charged nitrogen-vacancy (NV$^-$) centres in irradiated and implanted diamond, with two coherence records credited to removing them. Cluster-correlation-expansion simulations in which the spins outside each cluster keep exchanging spin projections in pairs reproduce the measured Hahn-echo coherence time of NV$^-$ centres in a substitutional-nitrogen bath to within 12%, inside the statistical uncertainty. Driven by published electron-paramagnetic-resonance parameters, the same calculation inverts the attribution. At a fixed paramagnetic spin density a multi-vacancy bath gives a Hahn-echo coherence time 3.0-6.1 times longer than a bath of isolated negative vacancies at 1 ppm, and 2.2-6.5 times longer from 0.01 to 10 ppm. A bath dephases the qubit because its spins exchange spin projections with one another, and two can exchange only if their transition frequencies match. A fine-structure splitting shifts those frequencies. Were every defect on the same crystallographic site, all would shift alike and still match, and the splitting would gain little, a factor 1.2. Real defects occupy symmetry-equivalent sites pointing in different directions, so neighbours land at different frequencies and stop exchanging: a factor 2.3. What governs the coherence time is therefore the fraction of bath pairs sharing a transition frequency, not the size of the zero-field splitting. Vacancy aggregation extends NV$^-$ spin coherence rather than shortening it.

This expanded Urdu-language review introduces classical and quantum game theory with particular attention to Nash equilibrium and evolutionary stability. It explains the role of quantum protocols, entanglement, admissible strategy spaces, and payoff equivalence, while distinguishing mathematical game-theoretic conclusions from claims of physical implementation. Detailed new sections distinguish equilibrium from ESS and from stability of payoff-equivalence classes, derive the instability of a classical mixed coordination equilibrium, discuss the Bloch-sphere quotient for a special quantum game, analyze noise and perturbations, and propose a reproducible research framework. The article ends with limitations and open research questions. .

The corresponding dual SDP further yields affine witnesses that can be used to rule out classical simulability. Applying the hierarchy to state sets under depolarizing noise yields computable upper bounds on the critical visibility. For several highly symmetric examples, these bounds are matched by explicit classical simulations, providing evidence for the practical usefulness of the hierarchy.

QRU leverages quantum controlled-SWAP (C-SWAP) gates to implement an information selection mechanism inspired by classical Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs), enabling selective processing of temporal information through quantum operations. The architecture features a measurement results feedforward scheme with shared parameters across time steps, achieving a constant parameter count and constant per-step effective quantum circuit depth (the depth of the effectively executed quantum circuit incurred over a single QRU time step) regardless of input sequence length. Across all tasks, QRU achieves 46.2%-99.7% parameter reduction compared to classical counterparts while achieving comparable performance. Preliminary hardware inference experiments on IBM quantum processors provide initial evidence of execution feasibility on real NISQ devices. The architecture's quantum-native design points toward a candidate quantum-native alternative to classical neural network components, offering a promising direction for parameter-efficient quantum machine learning as hardware capabilities and error mitigation techniques continue to improve.
