☆ Towards large-scale ab initio Molecular Dynamics Simulation with Efficient Sampling-based Quantum Computing Algorithms
Ankit Khandelwal, Nirmal M R, Aaryav Mishra, Debasmita Bhoumik, Dhinakaran Vinayagamurthy, M Girish Chandra
Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) requires the calculation of highly accurate electronic-structure energies and nuclear forces at every time step, which can quickly become computationally expensive. Sample-based quantum diagonalization offers a route to such calculations on quantum hardware, but its use in AIMD simulations has so far been limited to active spaces of about 20 qubits. In these spaces, exact diagonalization is tractable, and the quantum circuits are typically built from standard coupled-cluster amplitudes. Here, we introduce SqDRIFT-AIMD, which combines randomized sample-based Krylov quantum diagonalization (SqDRIFT) with analytical nuclear gradients. With SqDRIFT-AIMD, we obtain more accurate ground-state energies than the conventional coupled-cluster singles and doubles (CCSD) driven AIMD simulation for the $40$-qubit active space. We apply SqDRIFT-AIMD to study the dynamics of proton transfer in the Zundel cation, using circuits executed on IBM Heron r3 quantum processors. SqDRIFT energies fall below CCSD across the $40$-qubit double-well PES and stay within a few m$E_\text{h}$ of CCSD at 52 qubits. The $40$-qubit SqDRIFT-AIMD trajectory tracks the SHCI-driven proton transfer to within $1.33$ mÅ and exhibits excellent total energy conservation, with a standard deviation of only $0.245$ m$E_\text{h}$. These results extend quantum-centric AIMD to active spaces beyond the reach of exact diagonalization.
☆ Bridging Gaps with Tensor Networks: From the Haldane Gap and Beyond
Sirui Lu
Proofs generated by large language models are often difficult to understand, generalize, or formalize directly. Here we verify, digest, and formalize OpenAI's computer-assisted proof of a uniform gap in the periodic spin-1 Heisenberg chain using tensor-network diagrams and Lean 4. Reading the partition-function network along space and imaginary time shows how finite-ring bounds propagate across doubled lengths and inverse temperatures to all longer even rings, sharpening the spin-1 bound from the same finite inputs by a factor of 19 to $Δ_L > 0.0729$ for all even $L \geq 36$. We identify reflection positivity as the general condition behind the proof and certify uniform gaps in seven additional spin chains and ladders. More broadly, digesting machine-generated proofs into transparent physical mechanisms yields sharper bounds, broader theorems, and reusable formal verifications.

☆ Exact sampling beyond Fock inputs and linear optics: photon-number superpositions, photonic matrix-product states, adaptive and non-linear circuits
Jean Senellart, Stephen Wein, Pierre-Emmanuel Emeriau
Clifford and Clifford's algorithm samples single-photon boson sampling exactly, one output mode at a time, by adding the input photons in a uniformly random order. We extend this construction to other input states and to adaptive and non-linear circuits. It applies whenever non-negative weights on output prefixes and input sets satisfy one marginal identity, a set-chain lemma: the random-order sampler is then exact at one weight evaluation per candidate mode, and it gives the posterior over the hidden input set. We build four exact samplers on it. For sources in a superposition of vacuum and one photon, the weights are rectangular permanents on an offset input set, and the cost has the exponent of single photons under loss. For photonic matrix-product states of bond dimension $χ$, a gap-by-gap Kraus contraction turns each weight into a short sum of squared amplitudes. For adaptive linear optics, the chain starts from the posterior given the adaptive counts and rejects chains that contradict them. For a single-mode non-linear phase the identity fails, and rejection from linear branches is exact with acceptance $1/\|c\|_1^2$. All four samplers agree with strong simulation on small instances, and cost models put adaptive sampling with up to three adaptive modes within $10\%$ of single photons and a non-linear site at $\varphi=π/2$ at about $4\times$.
♻ ☆ Affine Equivalence in the Clifford Hierarchy
Jonas T. Anderson, Andrew Connelly, Mason Lovejoy-Johnson
In this paper we prove a collection of results on the structure of permutations in the Clifford Hierarchy. First, we leverage results from the cryptography literature on affine equivalence classes of 4-bit permutations which we use to find all 4-qubit permutations in the Clifford Hierarchy. We then use the classification of 4-qubit permutations and previous results on the structure of diagonal gates in the Clifford Hierarchy to prove that all 4-qubit gates in the third level of the Clifford Hierarchy are semi-Clifford. We then leverage results from \cite{He2024} to prove that all 5-qubit gates in the third level of the Clifford Hierarchy are semi-Clifford. We introduce the formalism of cycle structures to permutations in the Clifford Hierarchy and prove a general structure theorem about them, and classify many small cycle structures up to affine equivalence. Interestingly, this classification is independent of the number of qubits. Additionally, we show that all 1-wire-mismatch permutations are in the Clifford Hierarchy.
comment: 19 pages, comments welcome, v2: Table 3 complete and new method added for proving membership in CH for permutation gates
♻ ☆ When are bosonic Gaussian states classical to learn?
Senrui Chen, Antonio Anna Mele, Francesco Anna Mele, John Preskill
A fundamental question in physics is: When does classical behavior emerge from quantum systems? Bosonic Gaussian states provide a natural setting to explore this quantum-classical boundary, as they capture both the classical field behavior and the intrinsic quantum nature of light. Here, we address this problem from a learning-theoretic perspective by asking: When are bosonic Gaussian states classical to learn? That is, under what conditions (if any) can an n-mode bosonic Gaussian state be learned with as few samples, and with operations as simple, as are needed to learn a classical 2n-variate Gaussian distribution? We establish a smooth crossover in learnability governed by the state's thermal fluctuations: - Cold Gaussian states are non-classical to learn: When the covariance matrix satisfies $Σ\le(\frac12+O(\frac1n))I$, i.e. close to the vacuum covariance, tomography under single-copy (i.e., non-entangled) measurements fundamentally requires $Ω(n^3)$ copies, strictly exceeding the sample complexity $Θ(n^2)$ of learning classical Gaussian distributions. We show that this hardness persists even when few-copy entangled measurements are allowed. - Warm Gaussian states are classical to learn: When thermal fluctuations exceed the vacuum noise, parameterized by $Σ\ge(\frac12+ν)I$ for any parameter $ν>0$, we prove that single-copy tomography requires $N=Θ\left(n^2\min(n,1+ν^{-1})\right)$ copies. This bound is tight and is achieved by simple, non-adaptive, unentangled heterodyne measurements. Crucially, for $ν=Ω(1)$, the sample complexity drops to $Θ(n^2)$, matching the classical case. Our results tightly characterize a quantum-to-classical crossover in the learnability of bosonic Gaussian states, reveal a novel connection between fundamental physics and statistical learning theory, and have implications for real-world sensing experiments.

♻ ☆ Parallel Circuit Execution for Scalable Quantum Computation
Avimita Chatterjee, W. Michael Brown, Siyuan Niu, Wibe Albert de Jong, Thomas Lubinski
Today's quantum processors have tens to hundreds of physical qubits, but reliable execution of arbitrary circuits remains limited to fewer than 30 entangled qubits across hardware modalities. Building upon prior work, we introduce an error- and topology-aware method for mapping multiple independent circuits onto disjoint regions of a single large-scale QPU for parallel circuit execution. For applications with many similarly sized circuits, such as observable estimation for Hamiltonian simulation, this approach can reduce billed QPU execution time, with ideal speedup proportional to the number of usable partitions. We demonstrate the approach on IBM's 156-qubit ibm_boston processor using standard QED-C benchmark and Hamiltonian-based observable-estimation workloads. Compared with standard sequential execution, parallel execution reduces billed execution time by 3.5-5.5x while retaining 83-92% of the sequential fidelity. We further evaluate the scaling of parallel circuit execution using GPU-accelerated classical simulation, distributing measurement circuits across GPUs via MPI. Using CUDA-Q on the NERSC Perlmutter system, we achieve up to 13.8x speedup on 16 GPUs (86% parallel efficiency) for an H2 electronic-structure simulation, with scaling evaluated across multiple Hamiltonians and circuit counts. These results provide an indication of the performance ceiling that parallel execution on future quantum hardware may eventually approach. Both execution modes are implemented as a runtime option within the QED-C Application-Oriented Benchmark suite. Together, the results show that circuit-level parallelism can reduce execution cost on current quantum hardware and simulation time on GPU clusters, with the potential for greater benefits as device quality and qubit counts increase.

♻ ☆ Transmon Phase Gates Controlled by Superconducting Soliton DAC
Derek Reitz, Tony X. Zhou, Aditya Sharma, Ryan Bilotta, John McFarland, Aref Fouladi, Jacob Glasby, Aruna Ramanayaka, Zachary Stegen, Aaron Pesetski, Mark Covington, Gregory Boyd, Jeremy Clark
We introduce a superconducting digital-to-analog converter (DAC) that filters control noise, provides native multiplexing, performs quantum gates in nanoseconds, and can be controlled by CMOS. This is achieved by transducing a trapezoidal drive pulse into a superconducting soliton, which is then held in the DAC load loop, applying flux to a mutually-coupled superconducting qubit or gate coupler. The analog flux output by the DAC can be easily controlled by varying the soliton hold time, or with a DC-biased tunable DAC-qubit coupler, allowing the DAC to perform a fixed-time, high-fidelity gate that's robust to fabrication variance or flux offsets in the quantum circuit. Our initial demonstration shows that the DAC can successfully perform 5.6 ns S-gates on transmons. We measure the DAC-induced quantum state excitation probability per gate to be 0.05%, and find that the DAC-induced relaxation rate from the qubit 1 state is below the intrinsic T1 rate limit of the transmon. Quantum simulations show qualitative agreement with the measured data, and predict that the DAC excitation rate can be lowered 10 times further by overdamping the Josephson junction (JJ) in the DAC load loop. Interleaved Randomized Benchmarking (IRB) sequences on an observer qubit reveal that, when scaling to many qubits, the DAC's performance may be limited by a non-local, DAC-induced phase error of 1.6% per gate, appearing in ancilla qubits that are not directly coupled to any of the 30 DACs on the chip. We discuss strategies for future layouts of multi-DAC chips that focus on mitigating the source of these non-local, high-frequency electromagnetic interactions (EMI), and how to incorporate a DC-tunable coupler for phase correction.

♻ ☆ Quantum Temporal Marginal Problem
Dingqian Wang, Jiayi Zhao, Ge Bai
Experiments on a multi-time quantum process may reveal its responses only on selected, possibly overlapping, sets of times. We ask whether these partial descriptions admit a common underlying process, and formulate this process tensor marginal problem as a semidefinite feasibility test. Agreement on overlaps is necessary but insufficient: three locally consistent qubit marginals can have no common extension. Another family is incompatible as a time-ordered process even though a single quantum channel satisfies both its channel and temporal marginal constraints. This isolates temporal causality as the obstruction. We quantify incompatibility by the mixing needed to restore compatibility and derive finite tests using separate interventions at each time and final measurements. We further show that incompatibility is equivalent to an advantage over every compatible family in a multi-time process-discrimination task. Together, these results test whether process descriptions obtained in different experiments can arise from one causally ordered quantum process.

♻ ☆ Dynamical entanglement percolation with spatially correlated disorder
Lorenzo Cirigliano, Valentina Brosco, Claudio Castellano, Simone Felicetti, Laura Pilozzi, Bernard van Heck
The distribution of entanglement between the nodes of a quantum network plays a fundamental role in quantum information applications. In this work, we investigate the dynamics of a network of qubits where each edge corresponds to an independent two-qubit interaction. By applying tools from percolation theory, we study how long-range entanglement, obtained via singlet conversion and swapping from dynamically generated pairs, emerges across the network. We show that the interplay between unitary evolution and spatially correlated disorder leads to a non-standard percolation phenomenology, significantly richer than uniform bond percolation and featuring multi-valued hysteresis-like behaviour. A two-colour correlated bond percolation model, whose phase diagram is determined via numerical simulations and a mean-field theory, fully elucidates the physics behind this phenomenon.

♻ ☆ Highly resilient, error-protected quantum gates in a solid-state quantum network node
E. Poem, M. I. Cohen, S. Blum, D. Minin, D. Korn, O. Heifler, A. Hamo, I. Bayn, N. Bar-Gill, R. L. Patel, M. Markham, M. Tordjman
High-fidelity quantum gates are the cornerstone of any quantum computing and communications architecture. Realizing such control in the presence of realistic errors at the level required for beyond-threshold quantum error correction is a long-standing challenge for all quantum hardware platforms. Here we theoretically develop and experimentally demonstrate error-protected quantum gates in a solid-state quantum network node. Our work combines room-temperature randomized benchmarking with a new class of composite pulses that are simultaneously robust to frequency and amplitude, affecting random and systematic errors. We introduce Power-Unaffected, Doubly-Detuning-INsensitive Gates (PUDDINGs) - a theoretical framework for constructing conditional gates with immunity to both amplitude and frequency errors. For single-qubit and two-qubit gate demonstrations in a solid-state nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center in diamond, we tested the operation of the resulting protected gates at room temperature and find improvements above an order of magnitude. For a two-qubit CNOT gate, between the nuclear and electron spins, an error per gate of \mbox{$2.7\pm1.9\times10^{-4}$} is measured. Taking into account the increase in the electron coherence time at low temperatures, we predict that a two-qubit error per gate around $3\times10^{-5}$ is achievable. These results, far below the thresholds required by surface and color code error correction, thus present viable building blocks for a new class of fault-tolerant quantum networks.

♻ ☆ Sample-Efficient Quantum State Tomography for Structured Quantum States in One Dimension
Zhen Qin, Casey Jameson, Alireza Goldar, Michael B. Wakin, Zhexuan Gong, Zhihui Zhu
In this paper, we answer this fundamental question affirmatively by using a class of informationally complete positive operator-valued measures (IC-POVMs), including symmetric IC-POVMs (SIC-POVMs) and spherical $t$-designs, focusing on sample complexity while not accounting for the implementation complexity of the measurement settings. For SIC-POVMs and spherical 2-designs, we show that the number of state copies to guarantee bounded recovery error of an MPO state with a constrained least-squares estimator depends on the probability distribution of the MPO under the POVM but scales only linearly with $n$ when the distribution is approximately uniform. For general spherical $t$-designs with a sufficiently large $t$, we prove that only a number of state copies proportional to the number of independent parameters in the MPO is sufficient for a guaranteed recovery of any state represented by an MPO. In addition, we establish a sample complexity lower bound based on the Cramer-Rao bound, showing that, for strictly positive definite MPO states and unbiased estimators, a number of state copies proportional to the number of independent parameters in the MPO is also necessary, although the upper and lower bounds do not yet match in their dependence on the target accuracy. Furthermore, we propose a spectral method and a projected gradient descent (PGD) algorithm to solve the constrained least-squares problem, both equipped with rigorous recovery error guarantees.
♻ ☆ Dissipation of Spekkens' Generalised Contextuality under Decoherence: The Classical Limit
Enrico Bozzetto, Jonte R. Hance
When does a decohering quantum system become classical? Generalised noncontextuality gives one criterion, for scenarios rich enough in preparations: a system is classical once its statistics admit an underlying model in which operationally indistinguishable procedures are physically identical. Where it crosses depends not on the state and channel alone but on which preparations, transformations and measurements the experiment offers, and if every measurement is allowed there is no crossing. For any pairwise unbiased bases in any dimension, given preparations holding their eigenstates and surrounding the maximally mixed state, the question reduces to a finite linear program; for a qudit of odd prime dimension $d$ restricted to the stabiliser subtheory, with one depolarised magic state, we solve it in closed form. With preparations and measurements alone the qutrit strange state is classical at zero noise; with the Clifford gates added, each channel represented once, it crosses at 3/5; and with a random gate represented, as Spekkens' treatment asks, by the matching mixture of stochastic maps, at 3/4. A Clifford orbit of assignments supports such a representation only if it has $d^2$ members, leaving, in every odd prime dimension, only Gross's discrete Wigner function: the crossing sits where it stops being negative.

♻ ☆ Reduced State Embedding for Quantum Cryptography
Amit Kam, Kfir Sulimany, Shai Tsesses, Uzi Pereg
Encoding in a high-dimensional Hilbert space improves noise resilience in quantum information processing. This approach, however, may result in cross-mode coupling and detection complexities, thereby reducing quantum cryptography performance. This fundamental trade-off between correctness and secrecy motivates the search for quantum high-dimensional encoding approaches for cryptography. Here, we introduce state embeddings that use a k-symbol subset within a d-dimensional Hilbert space, tailored to the channel's error structure. We demonstrate the advantage of our scheme in realistic quantum channels, producing a higher secure key rate. We validate our approach using a d=25 quantum key distribution (QKD) experimental data, derive closed-form expressions for the key rate and threshold, and determine the optimum at k=5. These findings advance high-dimensional QKD and pave the way to error-correction and modulation for quantum cryptography.
♻ ☆ On the power of multipartite entanglement for pseudotelepathy
Gilles Brassard, Xavier Coiteux-Roy, Rémi Ligez
As early as 1935, Schrödinger recognized entanglement as "not one but rather the characteristic trait of quantum mechanics, the one that enforces its entire departure from classical lines of thought". Indeed, most remarkable phenomena in quantum information science, such as quantum computing and quantum teleportation, spring from clever uses of entanglement. Among them, pseudotelepathy enables two or more players to win systematically at some cooperative games with no need for communication between them, a restriction that would make the task impossible in a classical world. We investigate the power of multipartite entanglement for pseudotelepathy. Some known games that can be won with tripartite entanglement cannot be won with bipartite entanglement, but they can be won with bipartite nonsignalling resources such as the so-called Popescu-Rohrlich nonlocal box. We exhibit a five-player game that can be won with tripartite entanglement, but not with arbitrary bipartite nonsignalling resources even in the presence of arbitrary five-partite classical resources. This illustrates both the power of bipartite nonsignalling resources (over bipartite entanglement) and the even superior power of tripartite entanglement.

♻ ☆ Unifying Charge-Learnability Transitions in Monitored \(U(1)\)-Symmetric Quantum Circuits through Informational Power of Local Measurement
Yi-Fan Gong, Dan-Bo Zhang
Charge-learnability transitions in monitored symmetric quantum circuits reveal how local measurement records acquire sufficient information to infer a conserved charge. Here we extend charge learnability to probabilistic weak measurements, for which the measurement probability and measurement strength are independently tunable. We find that the learnability phase boundary is organized by the informational power of local measurement. We further introduce cross entropy as a label-sensitive diagnostic that distinguishes unbiased, biased, and antibiased decoder variants. Finally, the exact record--label mutual information provides a decoder-independent benchmark for the information fundamentally available for charge inference. Our results establish informational power of local measurement as a unifying principle for charge learnability under general monitoring protocols.

♻ ☆ The exact price of local realism in CHSH experiments: a measurement-dependence-detection trade-off surface, a moiré phase-locking mechanism that saturates it, and an unmeasured fringe in the fourfold coincidence sum
Aaron Alai
For local hidden-variable accounts of the CHSH experiment that are faithful -- reproducing the observed singles and coincidence rates and unbiased marginals of a polarization singlet with symmetric detector efficiency $η_{\rm eff}$ -- I determine the minimal measurement dependence $M$ (Hall's measure) needed to reach a CHSH value $S$. Linear programming over all local strategies yields $M(S,η_{\rm eff})=\max\{0,η_{\rm eff}((S+2)η_{\rm eff}-4)/6\}$, whose edges reproduce Hall's bound, the Garg-Mermin threshold, and the postselection ceiling. The quantum point is certified exactly: $M(2\sqrt{2},9/10)=(27\sqrt{2}-33)/100$, by primal and dual certificates in $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})$. I solve the detection profile under which a deterministic sign model reproduces the singlet exactly, and prove exact quantum correlations and angle-independent coincidence rates jointly impossible in this class. Mixtures of this profile with measurement dependence trade $M$ against a $\cos 4(a-b)$ modulation of the fourfold coincidence sum, up to 12.4% in relative amplitude, identical at the two CHSH angles; existing data exclude its full amplitude and bound its mixtures with flat detection to a detection share of order 15%; its sub-percent content is unbounded. A two-setting cross-ratio and a settings-torus log-Fourier protocol, calibrated against channel-efficiency imbalance, reach $5σ$ at 0.1% within hours; a flat result excludes the solved family to a detection share of order 1%. A local mechanism, moiré phase locking, with deterministic phase evolution and quenched randomness, attains the certified floor exactly at $η_{\rm eff}=1$ and, with the solved profile, reaches $M=0$ at $η_{\rm eff}\approx 0.80$. Its floor-attaining census shares a low-order Fourier skeleton across independent solutions and is not realizable by station-local offsets on the terrains tested.

♻ ☆ Time-Dependent Quantum Monte Carlo for fermions: from Bayesian conditioning to spinor dynamics
Ivan P. Christov
The time-dependent quantum Monte Carlo (TDQMC) method represents a many-electron state by an ensemble of replicas. Each electron is represented by a cloud of walkers sampling its density in physical space, with one walker and one guide wave per replica. The method replaces the Hartree potential with a conditional interaction constructed from the walker positions. Here, we derive this conditional interaction. By treating a walker as a finite-resolution localization of its electron, we show that Bayes' theorem, together with a single empirical substitution, leads to the Nadaraya-Watson form previously introduced on heuristic grounds. This form is recovered as an approximate Bayesian inference and becomes exact in the limit of vanishing resolution length. Because conditioning removes the gauge freedom that eliminates the orthonormality multipliers in Hartree-Fock theory, we enforce orthonormality through a term derived directly from the constraint. We further generalize the formulation to spinors, in which Pauli suppression at coincidence is graded by the local spin alignment. The resulting equations recover the established two-particle spin equations in the mean-field limit. For two electrons in a double quantum dot subjected to an inhomogeneous magnetic field, comparison with the exact solution shows that the spinor equations reproduce the non-collinear spin geometry inaccessible to collinear calculations. At strong exchange, determinant replicas recover most of the one-body entanglement entropy missing from a single-determinant description, although their spin contribution remains deficient. This deficiency is remedied by replicas constructed as the spin-coupled pair of valence-bond theory, which also reproduce the exact spin angle and singlet probability throughout the crossover between the exchange- and Zeeman-dominated regimes.
♻ ☆ Autler-townes energy-level engineering for high-quality all-microwave qubit gate
Wan-Peng Gao, Xiao-Liang He, Zheng-Qi Niu, Si-Qi Li, Da-Qiang Bao, Kuang Liu, Jian-Qiang You, Jaw-Shen Tsai, Zhen Wang, Zhi-Rong Lin
High-fidelity entangling gates are essential for realizing large-scale fault-tolerant superconducting quantum computing, yet existing approaches are limited: frequency-tuning techniques induce decoherence, while all-microwave-driven schemes suffer the trade-off between gate speed and leakage rate. Here, we introduce an energy-level engineering technique that employs the Autler-Townes effect to manipulate the nonlinearity of qubits without perturbing the computational subspace or degrading coherence time. This approach enables an experimentally validated, fast (97 ns) and high-fidelity (99.40(9)%) CZ gate, where error analysis reveals that gate errors arise mainly from static decoherence. The scheme facilitates fast, high-quality all-microwave gate operations with a simple topology and can be applied across various quantum platforms.
comment: This manuscript is the preprint version of an article published in Science China Physics, Mechanics & Astronomy. The final published version is available at: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11433-026-3065-5
♻ ☆ Bayesian-optimized magnetic-field-gradient sensing with a spin-orbit-coupled Bose-Einstein condensate
Shixiang Chen, Juan Wang, Yan Li
Building on our previous study of the expansion dynamics of a spin-orbit-coupled Bose-Einstein condensate, we propose a scheme for magnetic-field-gradient sensing that relates the maximum rotational deflection angle of the spin-density distribution to the magnetic-field gradient. We analyze the dependence of the sensing performance on key parameters and perform a systematic parameter optimization. A Bayesian optimization algorithm is introduced to efficiently identify the optimal parameter combination, thereby enhancing the sensitivity of magnetic-field-gradient sensing. Numerical simulations under the adopted noise model show that, compared with the parameter set used in our previous work, the optimized gradiometer improves the sensitivity by a factor of five. This work provides a new route for magnetic-field-gradient sensing and offers a reference for machine-learning-assisted quantum precision measurement.
♻ ☆ Protocols for a many-body phase microscope: From coherences and d-wave superconductivity to Green's functions
Christof Weitenberg, Luca Asteria, Ola Carlsson, Annabelle Bohrdt, Fabian Grusdt
Quantum gas microscopes probe quantum many-body lattice states via projective measurements in the occupation basis, enabling access to various density and spin correlations. Phase information, however, cannot be directly obtained in these setups. Recent experiments went beyond this by measuring local current operators and local phase fluctuations. Here we propose how Fourier-space manipulation in a matter-wave microscope allows access to various long-range off-diagonal correlators in experimentally realistic settings, realizing a many-body phase microscope. We demonstrate in particular how the fermionic d-wave superconducting order parameter in arbitrary Hubbard-type models, the non-equal time Green's function yielding the spectral function, or the hidden order of composite bosons in a fractional Chern insulator can be directly measured. Our results show the great potential of matter-wave microscopy for accessing exotic correlators including phases and coherences and characterizing intriguing quantum many-body states.
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures
♻ ☆ From Static Lindblad Stabilizability to Robust Physical Control Sequences
Yibin Wang, Ruifeng Liu
We derive checkable convergence, error, and execution-cost bounds for repeating a supplied finite control sequence from a static Lindblad stabilization certificate and complete implementation data, including concurrent background dynamics. The static decay bound and error bounds from static to planned evolution and from the plan to execution together bound the actual cycle's contraction factor in one fixed Lyapunov metric. For target-preserving planned and actual paths and a controller returning to its initial state each cycle, a uniform contraction bound below one gives cycle-end convergence from every initial state under cycle-varying uncertainty. Uniformly bounded within-cycle amplification in that metric extends this convergence throughout physical time when cycle durations are bounded above and away from zero. With leakage, uniform error bounds relative to certified target-preserving paths give explicit long-time distance bounds. Cycle and within-cycle bounds also screen a specified finite hardware library for sequences certified to meet and maintain a prescribed tolerance. In a four-level cascade with finite pulses, calibration and timing errors, always-on dephasing, and bounded pumping, the selected sequence brings every initial state within trace distance $0.1$ of the target in one complete cycle of explicitly bounded duration and maintains that tolerance under repetition.
♻ ☆ Sequential Capacity of Quantum Processes with Finite Memory
Yibin Wang
How complex can the responses of a quantum process become as it runs longer with fixed internal memory? We measure this complexity by sequential response capacity, the depth of an adaptive tree of experiments whose acceptance probabilities separate possible processes by a prescribed gap. Each experiment uses a fresh complete run, and one fixed process must realize every response along a path. For any fixed common visible dimension of at least two and internal memory cap, we prove that capacity has order $K\log((K+1)/γ)$ for $K$ transitions per run and probability gap $0<γ\leq1$. Time-dependent single-qubit phase channels without internal memory already attain the fixed-gap $K\log K$ growth, realizing each path with zero-or-one response probabilities. Under the same tester permissions, classical stochastic processes that measure in a fixed basis at every transition have only linear capacity at fixed dimensions and gap. For phase sequences selected by a classical address stored inside the process, we then quantify how known independent Pauli noise changes this logarithmic enhancement. With ideal tester controls and weak residual phase noise after correction, we prove matching capacity bounds at a fixed small gap. At fixed address size and fixed positive residual noise, the logarithmic enhancement saturates once the phase-sequence length exceeds the inverse noise scale, and capacity then grows linearly with sequence length.
♻ ☆ Noise redistribution by stabilizer codes: an organizing view of concatenated three-qubit codes
Long Huang
We formulate stabilizer-code error correction as a code- and recovery-dependent transformation of the noise channel. For a fixed recovery map, syndrome projection produces a block-diagonal logical channel whose diagonal Pauli weights follow from code-induced error classes, with no physical Pauli twirl; concatenation is then iterated redistribution, with the dominant logical error guiding the next code. The bit-flip and phase-flip three-qubit codes with standard recoveries supply a closed-form benchmark, and logically inequivalent recoveries appear as a design degree of freedom for shaping the channel presented to the next decoder. For amplitude damping, the three-qubit rules select C2(sigma_y)C1(sigma_x): one level converts the damping into a nearly pure logical-X channel at the price f1 = 1 - 3gamma/4, the second level suppresses that channel to f2 = 1 - (9/4)gamma^2, and the concatenated protocol overtakes the unencoded channel below gamma_c = 0.292 (f_c = 0.848); across the n-qubit repetition family the suppression order rises as gamma^(w+1), with w = (n-1)/2, while the gate budget grows as n^L. Correlated noise requires joint class statistics, whereas coherent noise retains intra-class coherences that make the same transformation usable in reverse as a tomographic fingerprint; there the companion work proves local identifiability from a rank certificate evaluated inside the parameter domain, classifies the sole permutation-symmetry ambiguity as structural at any chain length, and closes it with one two-qubit marginal channel. The construction remains an analytic benchmark, not a universal prescription for an inner code beneath a surface code.
comment: 9 pages, no figures. Companion paper: arXiv:2610.19779
♻ ☆ Breaking the Bounded Entanglement Barrier for Quantum Position Verification
Amit Behera, Vipul Goyal
Position verification, introduced by Chandran et al. (SIAM J. Computing 2014), allows verifiers to test a prover's claimed position by an interactive protocol. Classical position verification is impossible. Even for Quantum Position Verification (QPV), there always exists an LOCC (Local Operations and Classical Communication) attack if the adversary can hold an exponentially large amount of preshared entanglement. Somewhat surprisingly, we show that we can circumvent this barrier in the idealized continuous-time model, where time is represented by a real-valued parameter and challenge messages can be sent at a time sampled uniformly from a real interval. In this model, we give a BB84-based protocol that remains secure against any finite coalition of LOCC adversaries with arbitrary finite (possibly exponential) quantum storage and entanglement. Our construction can also be instantiated in the discrete-time model. Although prior impossibility results apply, our information-theoretic QPV protocol achieves any desired polynomial gap between the honest parties' total resources (communication and storage) and the adversarial resource bound. To our knowledge, all prior constructions that do not rely on idealized oracles required resources of the honest parties to be at least as large as the proven adversarial entanglement bound. Interestingly, the resource gap depends on the precision in measuring time. As clock precision improves, the adversarial resource bound increases while honest resources remain largely unchanged. We call this the "I sleep, you work" paradigm. Finally, we show that our techniques extend to an information-theoretic, position-based message authentication protocol, which in turn extends to an information-theoretic, position-based quantum key exchange protocol with the same guarantees as our position-verification protocol in the continuous-time and discrete-time models.
comment: Added extensions to position-based authentication and position-based key exchange protocols
♻ ☆ Imaging the topological sign of a Dirac mass with spin-polarized tunneling
Payman Kazemikhah, Ruolun Zhang, Byunghoon Kim, Xiangyu Luo, Zachary Ducorsky, Yu-Peng Zhu, Md. Shafayat Hossain, M. Zahid Hasan
A Dirac mass is characterized not only by its magnitude but also by its sign, which influences the Berry curvature, Hall response, and the propagation direction of chiral boundary modes. However, local spectroscopy of magnetic topological surfaces has so far accessed only the gap magnitude $|M|$. Here we show how the topological sign of $M$ can be determined locally. We first establish the sign information that spin-resolved tunneling can access and the reference required to obtain an absolute Hall sign. Although spin--orbital entanglement generally obscures the relation between measured spin and Dirac pseudospin, crystalline rotation symmetry alleviates this ambiguity at the band edge. On a $C_3$ axis, an axial tip couples to a fully spin-polarized state whose tunneling asymmetry directly reveals the sign of the occupied-band Berry curvature, independent of orbital composition. We further show that the zeroth Landau level provides an independent mass-sign measurement with an unpolarized tip, while opposite domains and their chiral domain-wall modes provide self-consistency checks. These results pave the way for imaging the locations where the topological character changes within a material, rather than merely identifying where a spectral gap appears.
♻ ☆ Quantum estimation theory with quantum noise control
Osamu Hirota, Masaki Sohma
Quantum estimation theory serves as one of fundamental backbones of quantum Shannon information theory and was mathematically systematized by pioneers of quantum information science. Although its applied research saw limited progress for a long period, the 21st century has witnessed active discussions and numerous fruitful proposals regarding its applications. Notably, the contributions of Monras and Paris represent one of the most remarkable achievements addressing the realization problem of estimation bounds. This paper aims to demonstrate a practical direction for extending their original ideas. Next-generation quantum information mechanisms urgently demand guarantees of quantum advantage unattainable by classical theory, alongside strict real-time processing without delays. By leveraging the concept of generalized heterodyne detection proposed nearly half a century ago, we demonstrate that a scheme based on their results can effectively meet the stringent requirements of near-future information technologies.
comment: Typos have been corrected. Appendices [C] and [D] have been added
High Energy Physics - Theory 20
☆ Decoupling Across Dimensions
Param Gogia, Caius Gordon-Bruno, Emily Nardoni, Peter Weck
We present a prescription for identifying decoupled sectors of 4d SCFTs obtained from compactifications of branes. Central to our analysis is the comparison of anomaly polynomials obtained via field-theoretic reduction versus anomaly inflow. Our flagship examples are the 4d $\mathcal{N}=1$ SCFTs obtained by compactifying the 6d $(1,0)$ theory from M5-branes probing a $\mathbb{C}^2/\mathbb{Z}_2$ orbifold singularity on a torus with flux. The anomaly polynomial of the interacting fixed point is known to decompose into the $T^2$ reduction of the 6d anomaly polynomial, plus a contribution from flip fields introduced to remove operators from the spectrum. Adopting the inflow perspective, the contribution from the flipped sector is obtained as the difference between inflow anomaly polynomials in the singular and resolved geometries, which we efficiently compute using equivariant localization. Helpfully, the 4d SCFTs admit two dual quiver gauge theory descriptions: $Y^{p,q}$ quiver gauge theories, and class $\mathcal{S}_2$ necklace quivers obtained from trinions. We study the interacting and decoupled sectors on both sides of the duality and construct an explicit map between their chiral rings, identifying a range of parameter space for which the quivers flow to apparently different interacting fixed points. Each chiral ring generator is furthermore matched to an M2-brane wrapping a 2-cycle in the resolved M-theory geometry.
☆ Nonlinear Scalarization of Reissner-Nordström Black Holes in Scalar-Torsion-Maxwell Teleparallel Gravity
Joaquín Robledo, Yerko Vásquez, P. A. González
We investigate the nonlinear scalarization of Reissner-Nordström black holes in scalar-torsion-Maxwell teleparallel gravity, in which the scalar field is nonminimally coupled to the Weitzenböck invariant. We consider polynomial coupling functions that avoid tachyonic instabilities at the linear level, thereby exploring a scalarization mechanism driven by nonlinear effects. In the decoupling limit, we study the nonlinear evolution of finite-amplitude scalar perturbations and show that the inclusion of a sixth-order coupling term allows the scalar field to dynamically evolve toward nontrivial stationary configurations. This behavior can be understood in terms of the effective potential, which develops nontrivial local minima that provide a mechanism for nonlinear saturation. By numerically solving the fully coupled field equations, we construct asymptotically flat charged black hole solutions endowed with scalar hair. We classify these solutions according to the number of nodes in the scalar field profile, identifying multiple branches whose structure and multiplicity depend on the coupling parameters. We further show that the higher-order coupling progressively suppresses higher-node branches and characterize the scalar backreaction through deviations of the metric functions and the torsion scalar from the Reissner-Nordström background.
comment: 14 pages, and 7 figures
☆ Projective symmetries and differential recursions for the large-$N$ Gross--Witten--Wadia and one-dimensional QCD matrix models
S. Voloshyn
We compare the fixed-charge planar Gross--Witten--Wadia (GWW) model with source-free one-dimensional QCD at large $N$ and $N_f/N$ fixed. In both models the resolvent and one-cut condition give an algebraic equation for a derivative of the free energy: a quartic for GWW and a sextic for QCD. Finite-$N$ Toeplitz determinants independently check the selected QCD branch. Signed permutations of homogeneous parameter triples realize $S_4$; the resulting action on the algebraic branches and operator labels gives a common projective description of the two models. For QCD, the sextic yields a differential recurrence linking small-charge rows two apart. The same second-order PDE gives a finite-width column recursion that reconstructs the coefficient pyramid from its GWW boundary. A distinct boundary, obtained from the first resummed coefficient, is the Narayana triangle. A formally collapsed slice counts decorated bipartite plane trees and admits an exact symmetric product formula. The many-flavor scaling reduces the sextic to the quartic and retains transverse projective data: the QCD divided-difference triple coalesces at this boundary, whereas the limiting quartic satisfies the full standard GWW third-order system. We distinguish algebraic degree, mixed differential order, and fixed-parameter ordinary differential order throughout.
☆ A geometrical approach for obtaining exact analytical solutions for a scalar field in a one-dimensional dynamical cavity
Maxwell F. de Araújo, Odemar Julião do N. Neto, Stanley S. Coelho, Jeferson Danilo L. Silva, Alessandra N. Braga, Danilo T. Alves
The dynamical Casimir effect was first predicted by G. T. Moore in 1969, who considered a real scalar field inside a cavity with a moving mirror in ($1+1$)D, satisfying Dirichlet boundary conditions. Moore wrote the general solution for the field in terms of a function that satisfies a functional equation nowadays known as the Moore equation.In the literature, exact analytical solutions to the Moore equation form a rather small set, restricted to specific classes of laws of motion. Cole and Schieve (1995) developed a geometrical approach that yielded a general formula for the solution of the Moore equation for cavities initially at rest. However, its application has always been done through numerical calculations, and their approach has therefore long been regarded solely as a numerical method. In this work, we show that their method can also be employed as a powerful method for deriving exact analytical solutions, and show the applicability of this approach to deriving analytical solutions to the Moore equation. We obtain original exact analytical solutions for an expanding cavity with a uniformly moving mirror, a contracting cavity with a mirror that approaches the static one asymptotically, and, in addition, we recover the first analytical solution to the Moore equation for a resonant mirror motion, originally obtained by Law in 1994. Moreover, we extend the Cole-Schieve approach, showing that exact solutions can be constructed from any spacetime region where the Moore function has already been determined. We show that this extended geometrical approach allows us to expand the set of known analytical solutions to the Moore equation from the few classes of motion reported in the literature to an infinite set, as it enables the treatment of new classes of laws of motion obtained by combining those presented here with each other as well as with previously known classes of trajectories.

☆ Liberation in the Heavy Limit
Sridip Pal, Gordon Rogelberg
We study CFT four-point functions of identical scalar primaries as their dimension $Δ$ grows for fixed $0

☆ Anomalous charge conjugation and parity in (2+1)-dimensional relativistic hydrodynamics
Sonali Patnaik, Rajeev Singh
We present a hydrostatic and first-order constitutive description of a mixed anomaly that involves $U(1)_Q$, $U(1)_F$, charge conjugation symmetry (acting only on $U(1)_Q$), and parity symmetry in $2+1$ dimensions. It is represented by a mutual Chern-Simons level $k_{QF}=\frac12 \,(\mathrm{mod}\ \mathbb Z)$. Adopting the already established multi-charge anomaly sector, we explicitly provide the information that this response is $odd$ under $\mathsf{C}$ and $\mathsf{P}$ symmetries separately, but $even$ under combined $\mathsf{CP}$ symmetry. We also provide a global inflow representative and compute the equilibrium cross-charge response which includes $\partial n_Q/\partial B_F=\partial n_F/\partial B_Q=1/4π\bmod 1/2π$. Using an analytic neutral-fluid example we show that this response is non-vanishing whereas the source-free hydrodynamic poles are invariant.
comment: 17 pages; comments and feedbacks are welcome
☆ The Fate of Collisional Neutrino Flavor Conversion: Fixed Points, Period Doubling, and Chaos
Jiabao Liu, Lucas Johns, Hiroki Nagakura
Core-collapse supernovae and neutron star mergers are among the most energetic astrophysical events and promising sources of multimessenger signals. Their dynamics and nucleosynthesis depend sensitively on neutrino transport, yet the impact of neutrino flavor evolution in these dense environments remains poorly understood. Predicting the outcome of collisional flavor instability (CFI) remains a challenge, despite progress in local-relaxation methods for fast flavor conversion. Here we construct homogeneous collective-precession states with stationary flavor populations in two-flavor quantum kinetics with collisional relaxation. The method applies to arbitrary energy spectra and energy-dependent collision rates. Our numerical examples exhibit persistent oscillations and a period-doubling route to chaos. Even in these regimes, the stationary populations estimate the time-averaged flavor populations to within $10\%$ in our tests. These fixed points provide a physically motivated input for incorporating CFI into astrophysical simulations, with implications for neutrino heating and ejecta nucleosynthesis.
☆ Gamma classes, central connection matrices, and tt* geometry
Martin A. Guest
We review the gamma class of complex projective space, but from the point of view of topological-antitopological fusion. We deconstruct the central connection matrix which appears in the work of Dubrovin, Galkin-Golyshev-Iritani, and Cotti-Dubrovin-Guzzetti.
comment: 25 pages
☆ Stanley Deser 19th March 1931 - 21st April 2023
M. J. Duff, K. S. Stelle
Stanley Deser was Ancell Professor Emeritus at Brandeis University and Visiting Professor at the California Institute of Technology. He was a world-renowned theoretical physicist whose accomplishments include the Arnowitt-Deser-Misner (ADM) formulation of general relativity, supergravity with Zumino, the dynamics of flat space with Jackiw and 't Hooft and many other contributions to the quantum theory of gravity. In the 1980s he was instrumental in securing National Science Foundation approval of the LIGO gravitational wave experiment against much opposition. He was awarded the Einstein Medal in 2015 for important contributions to general relativity, in particular the development of the ADM formalism. Other awards include: The Dannie Heineman Prize 1994; Fellow of the National Academy of Sciences 1994; Honorary Member of the Torino Academy of Sciences 2001; Member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences 1979, Fellow of the American Institute of Physics.
comment: To appear in Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society
☆ The first-order phase transitions and gravitational waves from an effective theory inspired by four-stack intersecting D6-brane models
Haotian Huangfu, Tianjun Li, Qi Sun, Rui Sun, Wenxing Zhang
First-order phase transitions in the early Universe can generate stochastic gravitational-wave backgrounds in frequency bands targeted by proposed deci-Hz observatories. We study the gravitational-wave consequences of the right-handed gauge symmetry breaking $SU(2)_{R_1}\times SU(2)_{R_2}\to SU(2)_R$ in a Pati-Salam effective theory inspired by four-stack intersecting D6-brane models. The ultraviolet construction fixes the gauge structure and particle multiplicities, while the scalar masses and quartic couplings are treated as renormalized inputs below the supersymmetry-breaking scale. Using a one-loop finite-temperature potential with ring resummation, we follow a strongly supercooled transition at the few-TeV scale through nucleation, percolation, completion, and reheating. The leading-order friction diagnostic does not support a runaway wall, so sound waves dominate the gravitational-wave signal, with turbulence as a sub-leading contribution; the finite acoustic lifetime suppresses the peak. For the fast-wall reference case, the spectrum peaks at $f_{\rm peak}=0.611$ Hz with $h^2Ω_{\rm GW,peak}=1.232\times10^{-11}$, in the deci-Hz band targeted by DECIGO and BBO. We present its dependence on the wall speed, renormalization scale, and thermal screening, together with a noise-only comparison for several proposed detector configurations.

☆ Quark-level CPT violation in neutral-meson systems
Ralf Lehnert, Agnes Roberts
This work investigates CPT and Lorentz breakdown in neutral-meson interferometry within the nonminimal Standard-Model Extension. Employing methods of chiral perturbation theory for mass dimension d=5, a connection between the quark-level and the meson effective pseudoscalar Lagrangian is established. The resulting phenomenological signatures in neutral-meson oscillations with particular focus on the detector geometry are explored. This analysis permits the interpretation of such CPT tests within the d=5 quark sector of the Standard-Model Extension. Existing data are used to extract first constraints on two coefficients and to estimate achievable sensitivity gains over published bounds of up to 18 orders of magnitude.
comment: 13 pages, 1 figure
☆ Kinematically Unrestricted Flat Space Scattering from AdS$_{d+1} \times$ S$^p$/CFT$_d$
Bhanu Narra
We construct scattering states for scalar fields with generic kinematics from CFT operators in the flat space limit of AdS/CFT. The states can have momentum along the compact $S^p$ directions of $AdS_{d+1}\times S^p$, which is achieved by scaling to large R-symmetry charge and choosing a particular parameterization for the R-symmetry polarization. These states allow for the construction of an unrestricted S-matrix from the flat space limit of CFT correlation functions, which we check for various tree level interactions. We also describe a generalization of the Mellin space formalism which incorporates the compact momentum, and we discuss some possible implications for flat space holography.
comment: 20 pages
♻ ☆ Quantum Charge-4e Superconductivity and Possible Deconfined Pseudocriticality in the Attractive SU(4) Hubbard Model
Zhou-Quan Wan, Huan Jiang, Xuan Zou, Shiwei Zhang, Shao-Kai Jian
Unlike conventional charge-2e superconductors, a charge-4e superconductor exhibits long-range coherence of electron quartets rather than Cooper pairs. Clear zero-temperature realizations of charge-4e superconductivity remain rare. Here, we investigate the zero-temperature phase diagram of the attractive SU(4) Hubbard model with numerically exact, large-scale quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulations overcoming major technical hurdles. We identify both charge-2e and charge-4e superconducting phases. Upon increasing interaction, charge-2e long-range order vanishes, while charge-4e correlations remain robust and converge with system size, establishing a quartet-condensed phase. Interestingly, across the charge-2e--charge-4e transition, single electrons remain gapped, while charge-2e correlations exhibit an effective anomalous dimension substantially exceeding the conventional O(6) Landau theory prediction. These features motivate a fractionalized framework in which the physical charge-2e order parameter is a composite field coupled to an emergent non-Abelian gauge structure. We formulate an Sp(4) gauge-Higgs theory associating the charge-2e and charge-4e states with Higgs and confined phases, respectively. A one-loop analysis of an SU($N_f$) generalization exhibits a fixed-point collision, motivating deconfined pseudocriticality as a possible interpretation of the observed scaling. Our results establish charge-4e superconductivity as a bona fide zero-temperature phase, provide a simple model for future studies in a numerically exact framework, and suggest an unconventional route to superconducting criticality.

♻ ☆ The Weight of $Spin(32)/\mathbb{Z}_2$ Little Strings: T-duality and Hasse Diagrams
Hamza Ahmed, Florent Baume, Paul-Konstantin Oehlmann
We study the worldvolume theories of stacks of $Spin(32)/\mathbb{Z}_2$ heterotic NS5-branes probing a transverse singularity $\mathfrak{g}$. We revisit and extend the original classification by Blum and Intriligator, and show that the resulting 6d Little String Theories (LSTs) are naturally labeled by affine dominant coweights of the singularity $\mathfrak{g}$. This in turn enables us to efficiently arrange these theories into groupings satisfying all known necessary conditions to be T-dual. Using this formulation, we then study the partial order of those coweights, and extend a recently proposed slice-subtraction algorithm to construct Hasse diagrams for LSTs directly from their six-dimensional generalized quivers, allowing us to probe certain properties of their Higgs branch. Along the way, we exploit these techniques to show that the number of duality orbits at maximal flavor rank is determined by the center of the transverse singularity $\mathfrak{g}$, and provide a simplified proof of a monotonicity theorem for this class of theories. Finally, we show how some of our techniques can be extended to other classes of 6d theories, such as Type-II LSTs and SCFTs.

♻ ☆ No Einstein Relation, No Problem: How Relativistic Weakly Coupled Heavy Quarks Equilibrate Beyond Leading Logarithm Anyway
Jean F. Du Plessis, Bruno Scheihing-Hitschfeld
Relativistic heavy quarks equilibrate even when their microscopic drag and momentum diffusion violate the Einstein relation. We investigate how equilibration proceeds as a function of the coupling and compared to simplified Fokker-Planck models. To do this, we present a detailed calculation of the momentum-transfer kernel in weakly coupled non-Abelian plasmas through strict $\mathcal{O}(g^4)$, and study the resulting dynamics at leading order in the inverse heavy-quark mass. Beyond leading logarithm, its non-Gaussian structure plays a crucial role in equilibration. We examine closely the analytic structure of the evolution kernel, determine the large-order asymptotics of the momentum-transfer cumulants, and show how the kernel's bounded analytic domain fixes asymmetric exponential tails at the level of the momentum transfer probability. Strongly coupled $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM also features an approximately Gaussian core and exponential tails, but differs in the nature of the kernel's singularities and the velocity dependence of the transport coefficients and tail exponents. These differences have distinct dynamical consequences: for the parameters studied, the persistence of the relativistic population in steeply falling spectra is largely explained by drag alone at very weak coupling, whereas fluctuation-induced survivor bias produces a large relative enhancement at strong coupling. Nevertheless, the shared qualitative structure between weak and strong coupling points the way towards a practical phenomenological description of heavy quarks anchored in first-principles field theory.

♻ ☆ MadStree: automated evaluation of tree-level de Sitter correlators
Jiaqi Chen, Yi-Xiao Tao, Xinyi Wang, Dong Zhang
We first derived the formulae of recursive reduction and d log-form differential equations for arbitrary tree-level and loop-integrand cosmological correlators, taking the external relations of massless bulk propagators into consideration. The differential equations could be systematically solved and provide the efficient evaluation of them. We have implemented this methodology as a Mathematica package MadStree. To demonstrate the efficiency of our method, we evaluated up to $10^6$ points for each master integral in our examples, and found that the average computational cost per numerical point per master integral is on the order of $μ\mathrm{s}$.

♻ ☆ Post-Newtonian theory in de Sitter and anti-de Sitter spacetimes
R. Loganayagam, Avi Wadhwa
We develop the post-Newtonian framework for the near-zone dynamics of a binary in de Sitter and anti-de Sitter spacetime. We consider a binary interacting via a free scalar field in a fixed (A)dS background in $D+1$ spacetime dimensions, with $D\ge3$ and odd. Using a novel multipole re-summation technique, we solve for the field degrees of freedom to obtain an effective particle description in the form of a Fokker action. We derive the equations of motion for the binary up to second post-Newtonian (2PN) order, and obtain the corresponding 2PN Hamiltonian and conserved charges in phase space. We show that the conformal algebra, corresponding to the isometry algebra of the (A)dS background, is realised in phase space as a curvature-dependent deformation of the Poincare algebra at each PN order. This serves as a non-trivial check on our results. Our results provide a systematic extension of post-Newtonian effective dynamics to finite-curvature backgrounds. This could serve as a useful framework for studying bound-state dynamics in (A)dS as well as in the corresponding holographic CFT.

♻ ☆ Holographic Pseudo Entropy from the Rindler Method in AdS and Flat Space
Mehdi Hakami Shalamzari, Zahra Paygozar, Mahdi Kord Zangeneh
Via the Rindler method, we study holographic timelike entanglement entropy (TEE) for a general timelike interval in AdS$_3$/CFT$_2$ and flat$_3$/CCFT$_2$. The TEE is the pseudo entropy of a timelike interval. In the bulk, the imaginary part of the TEE comes from a timelike geodesic. After a Rindler transformation to a rotating BTZ black hole, the two spacelike extremal curves lie on the inner and outer horizons, and exchanging $l_u\leftrightarrow \ell l_φ$ takes one to the other. We clarify the geometric role of the timelike extremal curve in the Rindler frame. We show that it is the line $\tilde U=\tilde V=0$ stretched between the two horizons, starting on the inner horizon, touching the outer horizon at its midpoint, and returning to the inner one. No such curve exists outside the region between the horizons. Its length, $iπ\ell$, is independent of the interval, and it alone produces the imaginary part $iπc/6$. We follow the same procedure in flat space holography, where the spacelike curve sits on the cosmological horizon and the timelike curve lies between the cosmological horizon and timelike infinity. Evaluating the holographic TEE for a timelike interval in CCFT$_2$ on the plane, we find that, in contrast with the cylinder, the real and imaginary parts are equal.

♻ ☆ Modular Flow and Holographic Timelike Entanglement Entropy in AdS and Flat Holography
Mehdi Hakami Shalamzari, Zahra Paygozar, Mahdi Kord Zangeneh
Timelike entanglement entropy provides a useful probe of holographic theories, yet an explicit bulk realization of the modular flow underlying its timelike extremal curve construction has so far been lacking. We construct modular flows associated with spacelike and timelike intervals in AdS$_{3}$/CFT$_{2}$ and extend this framework to flat$_{3}$/CCFT$_{2}$. Beginning with the boundary symmetry generators, we explicitly derive the boundary modular flows and extend them into the bulk, providing a systematic procedure that relates bulk modular flows to the extremal curves and holographic (timelike) entanglement entropy. For spacelike intervals, the resulting bulk modular flows determine the extremal curves, whose integrated line elements reproduce the standard holographic entanglement entropy. We then generalize this approach to timelike intervals, explicitly constructing the modular flows whose fixed points reproduce the extremal spacelike and timelike curves, which give the holographic timelike entanglement entropy. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first explicit construction of the modular flow associated with a timelike extremal curve for a timelike interval. The same procedure is then carried over to flat$_{3}$/CCFT$_{2}$, which gives rise to the holographic (timelike) entanglement entropy. Finally, we show that the flat space results obtained in this work can be recovered from their AdS$_3$ counterparts in the flat space limit.

♻ ☆ Critical and multicritical Kasner scaling in holographic phase transitions
Ling-Long Gao, Yan Liu, Hong-Da Lyu
We study how holographic phase transitions imprint their scaling laws on the local Kasner geometry inside Einstein-scalar black holes. At fixed double-trace coupling, we derive the near-critical scaling of the deviation of the first-epoch Kasner exponent from the Schwarzschild value: $p_t^{(1)}+\frac{1}{3} \propto O^2 \propto (T_c-T)^{1/r}$, where $O$ denotes the boundary condensate and $r$ labels ordinary criticality ($r=1$), tricriticality ($r=2$), and higher multicriticality ($r\geq3$). A super-exponential scalar potential generates a sequence of Kasner epochs separated by scalar-field bounces. We further find that any later epoch that can be tracked continuously across the transition inherits the same temperature exponent, while its coefficient depends on the epoch. Numerical solutions confirm these predictions for the ordinary and tricritical cases. Finally, we show analytically that the leading irrelevant exponent of the infrared fixed point governs the low-temperature Kasner scaling, and verify the resulting scaling numerically for the first Kasner exponent.

By numerically solving the fully coupled field equations, we construct asymptotically flat charged black hole solutions endowed with scalar hair. We further show that the higher-order coupling progressively suppresses higher-node branches and characterize the scalar backreaction through deviations of the metric functions and the torsion scalar from the Reissner-Nordström background.

Finally, rotating Nariai data admit the required spacelike graph throughout the regular branch; an all-order tensor estimate yields smooth Kerr--de Sitter or rotating-Nariai rigidity for $a^2/r_0^2\leq1/8$, without assuming ambient axial symmetry.

When the weights are nonnegative and the prefactor is one and the joint eigenspaces are lines, everything a probe reads off the spectrum depends only on the list of weights, which we call the profile. On the screen with equal weights summing to one the running dimension read by a diffusion probe falls short of two at unit time by at most twice the reciprocal of the number of qubits; a geometric profile gives instead, through its level count, a plateau of any positive height. Refining a grouping without end builds a tower whose boundary is a profinite set and hence a condensed set, on which a strictly positive compatible profile separates the locally constant functions by a distance. Applications certify probabilistic and strong contextuality and give the leading shortfall of the distance between the poles of the fuzzy sphere; in a model of monogamous entanglement the pairs that weight-one threads representing operational ER=EPR can occupy at once are exactly the partial matchings.

☆ Stanley Deser 19th March 1931 - 21st April 2023
M. J. Duff, K. S. Stelle
Stanley Deser was Ancell Professor Emeritus at Brandeis University and Visiting Professor at the California Institute of Technology. He was a world-renowned theoretical physicist whose accomplishments include the Arnowitt-Deser-Misner (ADM) formulation of general relativity, supergravity with Zumino, the dynamics of flat space with Jackiw and 't Hooft and many other contributions to the quantum theory of gravity. In the 1980s he was instrumental in securing National Science Foundation approval of the LIGO gravitational wave experiment against much opposition. He was awarded the Einstein Medal in 2015 for important contributions to general relativity, in particular the development of the ADM formalism. Other awards include: The Dannie Heineman Prize 1994; Fellow of the National Academy of Sciences 1994; Honorary Member of the Torino Academy of Sciences 2001; Member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences 1979, Fellow of the American Institute of Physics.

We investigate a minimal fractional deformation of Newtonian gravity as a unified effective framework for cosmology and weak-field gravitational tests. Here we demonstrate that a single-parameter fractional extension of the Newtonian action, motivated by fractal frameworks in field theory with a Stieltjes-type measure, gives rise to an effective framework capable of reproducing gravitational dynamics across vastly different scales. Previous studies of this framework have addressed cosmic evolution, including a nonsingular pre-inflationary phase, an inflationary attractor, radiation- and matter-dominated epochs, and the present accelerated expansion. The evolution of matter density perturbations has also been investigated, with results compatible with cosmological constraints. These applications share a unified effective potential description without introducing additional dynamical degrees of freedom. In this paper, we extend this construction to weak-field gravity, showing that key tests such as the perihelion precession of Mercury and the deflection of light grazing the solar limb are consistently described within the same potential, with all constraints pointing to only a small deviation from standard Newtonian dynamics. These results support a unified effective description of cosmological evolution and weak-field gravity, providing a basis for exploring the smallness of the effective cosmological constant, the hierarchy of Hubble scales, and the Hubble tension.

In the free field, uniformly bounded relative errors in the proposal mode variances give a volume-independent bound on the number of updates needed for a prescribed accuracy of the chain's stationary mode variances at fixed correlation length. It also provides access to the internal energy and magnetic specific heat, both usable as entanglement witnesses. For spin-$1/2$ trimers, we connect inter-multiplet inelastic spectral weight to genuine tripartite entanglement quantified by the concurrence fill. Finally, we reconcile the local character of IETS with its sensitivity to nonlocal entanglement through an analogy with digital quantum circuits, where Hamiltonian evolution implements multiqubit operations. Both changes travel outward. We solve this problem exactly for the Kitaev chain, the cluster chain in a transverse field, and the Kitaev chain with power-law couplings, and we find that far from the measured site every quadratic observable responds through a front. Where the front is and how fast it broadens depend only on the quasiparticle dispersion. How strong it is depends on two operators: how strongly the measured one creates the fastest quasiparticles and how strongly the observed one detects them; if either factor vanishes, the front is weaker and decays faster. One measurement therefore launches many fronts, one per observable, with a common position and width but different decay laws. In the Kitaev chain the density and the bond energy, the two terms of its nearest-neighbor Hamiltonian, respond to one density measurement with decay laws that trade places between the topological and the trivial phase; in the cluster chain, measuring a symmetry-odd spin instead of a symmetry-even one changes the critical decay law at a fixed Hamiltonian; and with power-law couplings the width law itself changes. All decay laws and profiles are obtained in closed form.

☆ Realizing Unstructured PDE Forecasting on Superconducting Quantum Processors
Erik Connerty, Jonathan Eastridge, Taylor Patti, Gerasimos Angelatos, Ethan N. Evans
Simulating high dimensional unstructured Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) with quantum processors is a major challenge with significant potential benefit. Existing methods have been demonstrated at small qubit counts, on simplifications of realistic problems. We implement a quantum reservoir network (QRN) for forecasting high-dimensional unstructured PDEs using up to 52 qubits on IBM superconducting hardware. Our method is gradient-free and does not suffer from the challenges of variational quantum algorithms. Instead, the QRN provides a large kernel space, up to 2^52 dimensions and beyond the reach of exact classical simulation, that remains useful under current hardware noise levels. Furthermore, a partial measure-and-reset mechanism enables total circuit runtime for ~24 times the qubit coherence time, so qubit lifetimes do not limit the forecast horizon. Thus, our method enables forecasting realistic unstructured nonlinear PDEs on quantum hardware. Typical difficulties associated with predicting large scale PDEs, such as transpilation, exponential shot requirements, hardware noise, and short qubit lifetimes are mitigated through careful design considerations and a dynamic observable reconstruction method. We validate our approach using a ~34k cell unstructured 2D cylinder flow at Reynolds number 1000 and a challenging nonlinear Gray--Scott reaction--diffusion problem, demonstrating high fidelity prediction on CUDA-Q simulation and on 26 and 52-qubit superconducting quantum processors. Specifically, we show that adding QRN features to an autoencoder linear prediction pipeline reduces prediction error by 21%-43%. Finally, we demonstrate closed-loop autoregressive PDE forecasting on these problems. This work demonstrates, for the first time, quantum circuits with depth beyond qubit lifetimes achieving accurate unstructured mesh forecasting on highly nonlinear PDEs.
comment: 27 pages, 26 figures
♻ ☆ ShardQ: Hardware-Aware Circuit Cutting and Recomposition for Quantum Data Encoding
Ziqing Guo, Jan Balewski, Steven Rayan, Kewen Xiao, Ziwen Pan
Quantum data encoding (QDE) loads classical data into quantum states and is a core primitive for quantum machine learning and quantum algorithms, yet executing QDE circuits on connectivity-limited noisy quantum processing units (QPUs) requires a compilation-and-reconstruction pipeline that partitions the circuit across the hardware and recombines the fragment outputs. Circuit cutting and knitting provide such a route, but the benefit depends on selecting a small number of high-value cuts because quasi-probability decomposition (QPD) incurs a sampling overhead that grows as $9^k$ for $k$ cut two-qubit gates. In this study, we introduce shardQ, a hardware-aware cutting and recomposition framework for structured QDE circuits with an address register, a data register, and an enumerable set of cross-register two-qubit gates under a chosen hardware layout. Its cut selector, SparseCut, ranks these candidate gates by hardware graph distance and selects a user-bounded cut set in $O(|\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{cross}}|\log|\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{cross}}|)$ time, avoiding mixed-integer-programming search in this restricted setting. The remaining truncated circuits are simulated with bond-dimension matrix product states (MPS), while the removed interactions are reconstructed using QPD on classical machines. Hardware measurements are the IBM Heron executions in Table I. Cut-finding, MPS, and overhead studies up to $150+$ qubit layouts are classical simulations or projections, and each such panel is labeled accordingly.

♻ ☆ A No-Go Theorem for Order-Two Clifford Electric-Magnetic Duality
Shunta Takahashi, Zhi Li, Beni Yoshida
Electromagnetic duality in the toric code has order two at the level of anyon types and acts as a Hadamard-type logical transformation on the encoded quantum information. Here, we ask whether it can likewise be realized microscopically as an order-two Clifford operation. For the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ toric code, we prove that any locality-preserving Clifford realization of electric-magnetic exchange cannot have order two. Our proof is fully general and requires neither translation symmetry with restricted families of system sizes nor a fixed pairing between vertex and plaquette stabilizers. Geometrically, the proof locally emulates the unavoidable crossing between electric and magnetic strings, similar to a cross-cap in a non-orientable manifold. Extending the problem to the $\mathbb{Z}_N$ toric code, we find that an order-two Clifford realization exists for odd $N$, whereas it is impossible for even $N$. Our result shows that the order-two exchange of closed-string operators cannot be extended to an order-two exchange of open-string operators.

♻ ☆ Relative entropy of entanglement and tripartite minimal surface
Takato Mori, Beni Yoshida
We propose a holographic dual of the relative entropy of entanglement for a boundary tripartition $A:B:C$. Our proposal is that, at the leading order, \begin{align} E_R(ρ_{AB}) = \frac{1}{4G_N}\Big[\mathrm{Area}(Γ_{\min}) - \mathrm{Area}(γ_{AB})\Big] \notag \end{align} where $Γ_{\min}$ is the minimal bulk tripartition surface and $γ_{AB}$ is the minimal surface homologous to $AB$. For a general random tensor network, we prove the corresponding upper bound by constructing a separable state associated with $Γ_{\min}$ and evaluating its relative entropy. We also establish the matching lower bound rigorously for networks of one, two, and three Haar random tensors by bounding the maximal tripartite product-state overlap. In appropriate geometries, the minimal tripartition surface can form a nontrivial tri-junction resembling the Mercedes logo.
comment: 55 pages, many figures
♻ ☆ On deep squeezing or cooling a parametric resonator using feedback
Adriano A. Batista, Raoni S. N. Moreira, A. A. Lisboa de Souza
Here we analyze ways to achieve deep subthreshold squeezing or cooling of fluctuations in a parametric resonator enhanced by a lock-in amplifier feedback loop. The main advance and novelty of this paper is that we analyzed the full impact of this feedback on the response of the parametric resonator to an ac drive or to additive noise. Due to this feedback, the dynamics of the parametric resonator becomes more complex and, in addition to a saddle-node bifurcation (SNB), a Hopf bifurcation (HB) at the instability threshold can also occur. We calculate the phase-dependent amplification gain in the response of the resonator to an added ac signal with three independent techniques: approximately using the averaging method (AM) or the harmonic balance method (HBM), and more precisely using Floquet theory (FT) and Green's functions. The HB was predicted by the AM, FT, and a modified version of the HBM that takes into account quasi-periodicity. In our analysis of fluctuations, we were able to calculate the noise spectral density and the squeezing or cooling of fluctuations using Fourier techniques and FT. Deamplification and cooling occur near the HB, whereas deep squeezing and heating occur near a SNB. Furthermore, we show that there is an optimal amount of parametric pumping and feedback to reach the strongest cooling. The theoretical framework presented here is general and could be applied to a wide range of physical implementations.

♻ ☆ Entanglement sharing schemes
Zahra Khanian, Dongjin Lee, Debbie Leung, Zhi Li, Alex May, Takato Mori, Stanley Miao, Farzin Salek, Jinmin Yi, Beni Yoshida
We ask how quantum correlations can be distributed among many subsystems. To address this, we define entanglement sharing schemes (ESS) where certain pairs of subsystems allow entanglement to be recovered via local operations, while other pairs must not. ESS schemes come in two variants, one where the partner system with which entanglement should be prepared is known, and one where it is not. In the case of known partners, we fully characterize the access structures realizable for ESS when using stabilizer states, and construct efficient schemes for threshold access structures, and give a conjecture for the access structures realizable with general states. In the unknown partner case, we again give a complete characterization in the stabilizer setting, additionally give a complete characterization of the case where there are no restrictions on unauthorized pairs, and we prove a set of necessary conditions on general schemes which we conjecture are also sufficient. Finally, we give an application of the theory of entanglement sharing to resolve an open problem related to the distribution of entanglement in response to time-sensitive requests in quantum networks.
